Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege of which I have given Your Honour notice. It relates to remarks made by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) at the time of consideration of questions on the motion for adjournment on Tuesday night. As recorded on pages 4476 and 4477 of Hansard, there are two references by the hon. member to a vote which was taken in the transport committee. The first reference, as recorded on page 4476, was as follows:
... or would he prefer to treat the opinion of the NDP on this issue, in view of their switch in position in committee, as indicative of public opinion.
Further, as recorded on page 4477, he said:
... or will the government continue to push blindly ahead, bolstered by the votes in committee of NDP members who in a moment of utter hypocrisy voted on estimates to give the government the money to push ahead with this unnecessary project?

speechtext:
My question of privilege is based on two points, Mr. Speaker. First, the hon. member's remarks are a reflection on a vote in a committee and as such are improper remarks to be made in the House. Second, the hon. member's remarks, particularly the second statement, involve an imputation of motives on the part of another member of the House.
The hon. member for St. Paul's can say anything he wishes outside the House about me, my colleagues or our votes in the House, but in this chamber he should respect the traditions of the House and neither reflect on a vote nor impute motives on the part of another member.
The substance of his imputation is that, although opposed to the building of the Pickering airport, I voted for the appropriation so that the government could go ahead and pay those people who wished to be expropriated. He is interested in supporting this as a change of position on my part that took place not only in terms of months but on the same day.
To end my point, I could very well in this House point out to the hon. member that he, in committee, in relation to his motion which he claims correctly I did not support, stated, as recorded on page 5:77 of Issue No. 5 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications:
Mr. Chairman, the members should be perfectly clear that this motion does not kill the Pickering airport.
It was clearly stated by him that his motion was not in opposition to the Pickering airport.
On this matter, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask for a withdrawal of the hon. member's remarks of the other night.

subsubtopic: PACIFIC WESTERN AIRLINES APPLICATION TO SUBCONTRACT CERTAIN ROUTES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, namely, the arrangement by the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission for a public hearing in Vancouver on June 18 into an application by Pacific Western Airlines to subcontract some of its routes to other air carriers and the fact that the Air Transport Committee gave insufficient notice to those who may want to make some preparation and appear at that hearing. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
This House calls upon the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission to postpone its scheduled hearing relating to the request by Pacific Western Airlines to subcontract some of its routes in B.C., which hearing is scheduled to be held in Vancouver on June 18, in order that interested parties may have adequate opportunity to prepare for the hearing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a very pleasant day. It is an appropriate day for a trip to sea as long as we do not get too far off shore or lost at sea.
This motion is placed before the House today to give members an opportunity to indicate their support for the position and, indeed, the principle that Canada and other coastal states own the fisheries resources on and over their respective continental shelves and slopes, and that the management of these fisheries resources are the responsibility of the coastal state. It is important that we indicate our support for our position in view of the forthcoming Law of the Sea Conference and, without injecting too much controversy, we wish to discuss some of the misrepresentations made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) with regard to general views on this subject in this country. I simply wish to open the subject. A number of my colleagues will want to develop the points that I make as well as develop further points.
Fisheries
Those of us who have grown up by the sea have been involved in coastal life, associated closely with fishermen and the kind of life they lead, and are aware of the vast potential of the sea as a source of wealth as well as of the importance of the supply of fish to our fishermen. We are intensely aware of the vital importance of preserving the stock of fish, as well as the increasing pressure from many sources upon this great reserve of wealth as a result of technical innovations and vessels from various countries being able to move further afield, particularly factory ships. We are aware also that this increased pressure is not confined to our traditional fishing areas, but is a phenomenon that is being very keenly felt elsewhere.
I, of course, am identified particularly with the east coast of this country and the fishing problems there. However, I am familiar with the problems on the west coast and the measures that have been taken over recent years to at least cope with these problems. I am familiar with the disputes and difficulties that still remain, as well as with the general state in which they are today.
It is the east coast that I know best. I am familiar with the jurisdiction in eastern waters and the extension further to sea as well as the inclusion of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I am aware of the importance of this. However, I am only too familiar with the depletion in the stock of fishing species in the region over which we are claiming jurisdiction, namely our continental slopes and shelves. I am well aware of how difficult it has become for fishermen to make economic catches, despite very significant improvements in their equipment. Anyone who sits in this House must be aware of the depletion of many species as well as the often expressed fear of the extinction of certain species.
Many times my colleagues in this House have demanded action and protection for our fishermen and offshore fishing grounds. They have expressed concern about the share of available fish to be harvested by Canadian fishermen. I think I know what has been going on under the jurisdiction of ICNAF. Moves have been made to establish quotas. I think that a quota on herring is in operation. I believe that quotas are now in effect for other species such as cod, haddock and flounder and quotas for other species are under consideration.
I do not rise today to carp or be critical. However, I think these efforts have been a very long time in coming. I do not think there is any reason to believe these quotas will really work. I say this because of the slowness of this process. There is concern as to whether these arrangements will really work in terms of conservation or whether they will take care of the needs of Canadian fishermen. Because of this, some time ago my party turned to a consideration of the extension of Canadian jurisdiction over the waters over our continental shelves and slopes. We turned to the principle of Canada achieving that jurisdiction and exercising management of the fishing stock in the waters over our continental shelf and slopes.
I agree in principle that there is something attractive about the idea of a truly international approach to the problem of conservation. There is something attractive about the idea of nations being able to work together to achieve agreement, to achieve some joint means of surveillance and enforcement, to achieve an equitable sharing of
4532

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
the marine resources of the world. But the idea really does not seem to be working, either in terms of management or in terms of surveillance, and there does not seem to be much prospect of much success in the future to judge by the way things are going.
I could not help noticing an article in the Economist, dated June 2, devoted, basically, to the dispute between Britain and Iceland. The article reviews the general situation, speaks about the erosion of the doctrine of the freedom of the seas, speaks about preliminary consultation already going on in preparation for the San Diego conference and says that very few governments have shown any real interest in fair sharing of supplies or in the preservation of the marine environment. The article goes on to say, and I quote:
Much of the current excitement turns on claims to national authority in the "superjacent" waters that lie above the continental shelf and slope zones off the coastal states' shores. Australia and New Zealand are thinking of claiming authority over a 200-mile zone; several South American states already make similar claims; Morocco is now violently at odds with Spain over its 70-mile claims; Iceland has indicated that it will soon extend its claim to 70 miles; and so it goes on, with China even demanding the scrapping of the 1958 and 1960 conventions, which it denounces as the product of imperialist machinations.
Then follows what is, to my mind, the most interesting part of the whole article, particularly since it is devoted basically to the dispute between Britain and Iceland and the right of British fishermen to fish in waters off the Icelandic coast.
If the trendy thing is going to be for each coastal state to grab all it can, there is not much to be gained-and there may be much to be lost-by a solitary attempt to buck the trend. It is probably time for Britain to start preparing for the 1974 conference by deciding how far out it will push its own maritime frontiers-and then enforce them.
Now, for a perceptive economic journal to take this position in the context of the dispute which is going on between Britain and Iceland indicates how much the thinking has changed with regard to this whole situation and how far disillusionment has set in as to the prospect of any satisfactory regulation of these matters by international arrangement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
This may be regrettable. As I say, there is something attractive to me about international regulation and co-operation, but to date at least the ICNAF arrangements have not in my judgment effectively protected the species or done the job that needs to be done to manage these marine resources properly. As Canadians, we want to be good citizens of the world but it is certainly our duty to protect our fishermen and to conserve the stocks of fish off our shores. Pressure on these stocks has been increasingly heavy. There is, too, I am told, inadequate surveillance of these waters-insufficient protection of our fishermen and fisheries. I have no doubt other speakers will emphasize this aspect.
So it was to protect our national interest and to protect our fishery stocks that my party adopted a resolution in Charlottetown last autumn which called, first of all, for the re-establishment of a separate department of fisheries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
The resolution then went on to say, and I quote:
-under this new department, launch a new, aggressive program to extend Canada's managerial control to the extremities of its continental shelf, for conservation and management of its marine resources; immediately increase its surveillance and protection capabilities for the fishermen ...
This principle was adopted as a matter of national policy.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate sought to get the Secretary of State for External Affairs to indicate support for the principle behind the position being taken by Iceland. I do not know how happy the Minister of Environment and Fisheries is with his title, because he tried pretty hard to get "Fisheries" expunged from it. Anyway, he made a political speech

June 7, 1973

before a Liberal association in New Brunswick the other evening, no doubt trying to generate a little enthusiasm for his party in a difficult part of the country. I quote:
And where do our Conservative friends stand now? They are boldly talking about a fifty mile limit. Little Iceland is going for fifty miles so Canada might be so bold to do likewise. That is Conservative thinking for you.
I simply indicate to the House that, because of our disillusionment with the effectiveness of international arrangements such as ICNAF, we in this party last fall formally adopted the resolution I have read. I think it must be the fault of the organization. I do not think it is the lack of drive which the minister has put into Canada's participation in that organization, and so it must be because of the lack of success of that organization, or at least partly for this reason, the minister has turned to the idea of making a vigorous demand to the Law of the Sea Conference for the extension of our rights to the waters over the continental shelves and slopes.
As a matter of fact, I think it was a rather cheap shot that the Minister of the Environment took when he was in New Brunswick, but I recognize the dire straits in which he must have been down there in trying to generate a little excitement in his party. I say to him that he had better get on with the job and, if he does, he will get lots of support over here. I think he had better get ahead with the business, within ICNAF, of protecting species, at least while we are relying on ICNAF. He had better get ahead with the job of providing adequate surveillance, because surveillance seems to be very inadequate today. Indeed, Sir, if I may give him a little advice, which I hope he does not find offensive, it might be more helpful for the fishermen if he did get ahead with the job of providing the surveillance that is needed, and providing the protection that is needed, instead of talking so much about it.
I simply want to say this in closing: we want to see the protection; we want to see the conservation; we want to see the management by Canada of our marine resources in the waters over the continental shelves and slopes. Those of us who live by the sea do not enjoy seeing the minister playing games with the matter. We want to see him get on with the job, and we will support him.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise and indicate the support of the New Democratic Party for the motion which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has placed on the order paper for our consideration today. I think it is important to recognize that when a motion of this kind is put before the House it represents some forward advance in our thinking in the area of preserving the resources of the sea that are adjacent to our coasts.
I think it would be well if we, as members, were all prepared to admit that over a period of years we have been groping towards a more adequate way of conserving those resources and protecting the rightful interests of Canadians who go down to the sea to fish.
I thought the Leader of the Opposition exercised very commendable restraint-perhaps it was his style of speaking-in reference to the speech delivered at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, last May 26 by the minister. Obviously, it was a political speech. Far be it from me to suggest that ministers of the Crown should not from time to time make
Fisheries
political speeches. But, Mr. Speaker, the notes for that speech were distributed to us on the letterhead of the Minister of Fisheries for Canada, and when we get them in that form they lead us to hope that at least basically they contain serious statements of policy. As I say, it is self-evident it was a political speech, but the point that needs to be clarified in this chamber, and it has not yet been clarified, is to what extent that speech represents the official policy of the government of Canada.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). I certainly agree with him that it is high time the Secretary of State for External Affairs got up in his place in this House and gave us his views, in such a way that we could recognize exactly what Canada's foreign policy is in the realm of developing an approach to the law of the sea that will protect Canada's interests. It seems to me that often such matters are shoved off on to the Minister of Fisheries, and not enough recognition is given to the fact that in this area at least we, along with other countries, are involved in a great many important matters that vitally affect our interests, and indeed the future resources that will be available in terms of high protein foods to feed a hungry world.
When I first came to this House we were really in a different era. At that time, Canada dealt with this question, and it is only fair to say we did not do too badly, through bilateral treaties or arrangements. By and large, the encroachment of other nations with modernized high-seas fishing fleets had not yet come into being. So, we had bilateral treaties. Later, it began to be apparent that that approach was not adequate. It became apparent that we had to have a new look at where, either ourselves or in concert with other nations, we should assert increasing jurisdiction.
I was quite dismayed by the speech which the Minister of Fisheries made in St. Andrews, New Brunswick, because undoubtedly it was most unfair and not a factual attack on the position which the Conservative party is currently enunciating. If there is any one matter on which this House should try to set aside any narrow, partisan considerations and speak with a united Canadian voice, it is on this matter of our position on our jurisdiction over the resources of the sea.

speechtext:
I hope the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will clarify, during this debate, whether the rather extravagant remarks made to the Charlotte-Carleton Liberal Association do represent the position Canada is taking at the Law of the Sea Conference looming ahead. It is not my business to interfere with that question of which kettle is calling which pot black, but in this context I cannot help but draw the attention of the House to a little item that appeared in the Ottawa Journal on May 31 in which Mr. Henry Heald says:
If anyone can claim kudos for far-sightedness in pushing out fishing limits, it should be Frank Howard (NDP-Skeena) who was calling for bold advances before Mr. Davis was ever elected to parliament. He was a constant prod urging the government to take the bold step of replacing the old three-mile limit with a 12-mile headland-to-headland fishing zone.
4534

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
Perhaps the Minister of Fisheries' perspective is understandably a bit foreshortened on this matter because he has not been in the House that long, but I took the trouble to look at Hansard for the year 1960 and I think perhaps one of the first references ever made in this House to the extension of our territorial waters was made on June 29, 1960 by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), as reported at page 5565:
Perhaps the most appropriate thing to do, so far as our general limits are concerned, is to take unilateral action and declare as Iceland has declared and as others are considering now, that our territorial limits for all purposes are 12 miles, and that is that.
It is surprising how often Iceland crops up in discussions of this matter. One can follow this course of events through the years. I might point out that in the next year, 1961, the member for Skeena introduced Bill C-96, to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, to provide for a 12-mile fishing zone in Canada.
When I returned to this House and rejoined the hon. member for Skeena on the fisheries committee, there was a question then as to who was outdoing whom on the matter of how timid we could be in the steps we were prepared to take regarding our fishing zones, the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Fisheries or the Official Opposition. However, I suggest that question is not really pertinent today because the motion before us clearly indicates our changing thinking on the matter of exercising jurisdiction over the continental shelf.
If I may, perhaps I could just blow my own horn a little bit. In 1970 when we had Bill C-203, to amend the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act, before the House I moved an amendment which had the effect of doing exactly what is envisaged in the resolution now before us. It was not accepted by the House, and to the best of my knowledge it was supported only by my colleagues in the NDP. My amendment read:
The fishing zones of Canada comprise all water adjacent to the coasts of Canada, the natural resources of whose subjacent submarine areas Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit-
I took this rather awkward phrase from the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act as the definition of the continental shelf envisioned by the government of Canada. I hope we can have an indication from hon. members on the government side of their preparedness to recognize the position of the opposition, and that they will support the opposition in exercising our jurisdiction in respect of the continental shelf.
There is one rather important omission in the text of the motion put forward by the Leader of the Official Opposition. One of our most important fisheries, namely the salmon fishery off the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, would not be protected merely by asserting Canadian jurisdiction to the edge of the continental shelf. We all know that salmon roam abroad in the high seas and return to our coasts and our rivers to spawn. If we are to consider this whole matter in its full context it is necessary to propose, in addition to the motion now before us and I intend to move an amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Olaussen), an extension to our jurisdiction. I therefore move:

That the motion be amended by adding a comma following the words, "with the permission of the coastal state" and inserting thereafter the following:
"and asserts ownership by Canada of anadromous fish spawned within our borders, and the exclusive right to harvest the same."
I think I have already made it clear, but for those who may not be familiar with that particular term, let me say that for all practical purposes this refers to our salmon fishery. In this connection, we recognize that on both coasts one of our richest fisheries and the most highly regarded species is the salmon. Unless we are prepared to recognize the principle that when these salmon are feeding in the high seas they are still considered as Canadian fish, in the long-run we cannot assure their protection, and cannot assure that the money we may invest in developing and conserving their propagation will not be wasted. I feel this is one of the important principles Canadians should be endorsing.
I remember suggesting in this House a number of years ago that we might say when these salmon are in the high seas they carry our brand. We should treat them in the same way as cattle were treated in the days of the old open range. The range lands were open, not the property of any one cattle ranch and, since the cattle were branded with the owner's name, they were permitted to roam. Then, at the appropriate time, they were rounded up. As we can all recall, it was a very serious offence to engage in cattle rustling, and I suggest that Canada should be saying that we do not want anyone rustling our salmon. I understand that our scientists now have the technical ability to identify salmon by their scales in somewhat the same way as human beings are identified by their fingerprints. We can now identify salmon in the high seas as being, in fact, our salmon.
I cannot help feeling that the minister has been unnecessarily using some of our commercial fishermen as pawns in this game, and my opinion is shared by others. I should like to make a brief reference to a letter which appeared in the Evening Times-Globe, Saint John, New Brunswick, on February 21 last. It was written by A. G. Huntsman, Professor Emeritus of Biology of the University of Toronto. He is sometimes referred to as the "father of fisheries research in Canada". In that letter he says:
When the ban on New Brunswick commercial salmon fishing was announced last April, I at once wrote to the minister that he was doing a very foolish thing, to stop the fishing without scientific evidence of overfishing and then to spend public funds to compensate the fishermen.
This may be a debatable point, Mr. Speaker, but from what I have been able to learn, the fact remains that it was not the commercial fishermen of the Atlantic coast who were responsible for the depletion of our salmon. When one considers what may have happened one is led to the belief that the industrial activities of others resulted in the depletion of our salmon. The other day the minister was talking about the amount of money being spent for research and development of the Canadian fishery and the fact, that it is much more than is being spent on agriculture. The minister made two errors. One was that constitutionally the fisheries are under federal jurisdiction, and he ignored what the provinces may have spent on agriculture,
June 7, 1973

on forestry resources and so on. Second, he ignored the impact upon our fisheries of other industrial activities which quite properly should bear a share of the cost of preserving and expanding our salmon fishery at its source in our rivers.
The only other point I should like to make, if I have time, has to do with the current situation in respect of our Pacific salmon. We have been having some discussions with the United States authorities. According to the minister and other spokesmen who have been following these discussions, the United States has been pretty tough with us. I suggest it is about time we started shoving a few facts down the throats of our United States friends because they refer to the Columbia River as if it were their river.
The United States apparently is not prepared to admit that it has robbed Canada of its share of the Columbia River salmon. If the United States is now producing salmon in hatcheries in the lower reaches of the Columbia River, it should recognize that a fair share of this salmon rightfully belongs to Canadian fishermen. The United States authorities should cease this nonsense of trying to establish their claim to the Columbia River salmon and, at the same time, demand half of the Fraser River salmon. The United States-and this came out in the 1964 hearings on our territorial seas bill-has a solemn treaty with Canada which the then Secretary of State for External Affairs told me was still in effect, the Oregon Treaty, which guarantees us our rights on the Columbia River, our right of navigation forever from the 49th parallel to the mouth. The United States stands in flagrant violation of the terms of its solemn treaty. In that connection, when the Grand Coulee Dam was built it not only cut off navigation on the Columbia River but also, and incidentally at the same time, killed off all the Canadian salmon which previously had spawned in the Canadian part of the Columbia River.
When one starts talking about a respect for the right to the salmon which originate in the streams of a coastal state, this is an important point which we should be making with the United States, and which, in all fairness, I do not see how it can ignore. This issue, I suggest, must be faced in our dealings with the United States and, hopefully, the United States may be prepared to recognize the justice in our position. I believe the United States is concerned with the basic principle which my amendment suggests should be endorsed by the House. If the United States is to have jurisdiction over the salmon which originate in its streams in Washington, Oregon, California and Alaska-I shall not mention the Atlantic salmon because I do not think the United States has any left; they killed them all off quite a while ago-it must also first recognize that Canada must have that same right and, second, that when it talks about the Columbia River it is talking about not a United States river but an international river. I put forward this suggestion in the context of this debate because I think it is the type of issue which will have to be sorted out as we move into the final discussions of the upcoming conference on the Law of the Sea.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent events relating to the problems facing Icelanders and
Fisheries
Britishers in connection with coastal fishing have prompted the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to introduce a motion which, I must admit, is timely and deserves our utmost consideration.
In my view, the amendment which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) has just moved complements the motion of the leader of the official opposition.
Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that a country like Canada, which has vast openings on the Pacific and on the Atlantic oceans, needs legislation that can guarantee both autonomy and respect for fishing rights along the coastlines so that they can really be applicable and applied.
As regards the Gulf of St. Lawrence for instance, I happen to know that many fishermen were complaining precisely about the fact that, because of the lack of regulations, anybody could come in these waters and catch the fishes which happen to be there. We have to remedy the absence of regulations or the lack of means of implementation. The motion asks for the recognition of, and I quote:
. . . the principle that Canada and other coastal states own the fisheries resources on and over their respective continental shelves and slopes, that the management of these fisheries resources are the responsibility of the coastal state, that other states may only fish such resources with the permission of the coastal state . . .
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps it has now become urgent that we get concerned with developing relevant rules which I could qualify as being rather severe.
We know very well that we have here in Canada immense resources of every description, including fishing resources, but we should not be careless and run the risk of losing them progressively simply because of a faltering sense of responsibilities.
It is thus quite natural, as indicated by the motion before us, that we agree to implement this policy of:
. . . adequate surveillance so that swift action can be taken when Canadian interests are threatened or violated.
Before being driven to major conflicts, it should be very important that we spell out clearly and categorically our country's position concerning coastal fishing rights. And the more quickly we do this, the better we will be able to avoid all kinds of problems like those between England and Iceland.
I therefore think that the government should very seriously consider accepting this motion so that we may be assured that Canadians will really be masters in their own home and will be able to have the whole population benefit from controls guaranteeing our ownership.
This is why I approve the motion moved by the NDP member. In fact, should we accept these two principles, we would have adequate legislation, favourable to the whole of Canada. It would not be a matter of requiring respect from others but by being consciencious and adult enough to take our responsibilities we would deserve the respect of other countries and we would not have to face serious difficulties likely to tarnish our reputation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment and Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome, and I am

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
sure all hon. members of the House welcome this opportunity to discuss the fishing limits of both our coasts. It is a very important matter, not only for fishermen but for Canadians. It is a matter which verges on sovereignty, but it also has a great deal to do with wise management and conservation of many of the world's living resources of the sea.
Canada has the second longest coastline in the world; it has the world's largest continental shelf, and it is, I believe, the duty of Canadians to manage the living resources along its vast coastline out over its vast shelf, not only in the interest of our own people, but in the interest of all mankind.
The resolution before the House goes some distance down the road toward permitting the wise management of the fish and other wild living things out over our continental shelf. I am glad to see that the resolution mentions the slope as well as the shelf. We must concern ourselves with management of fish over the whole of the shelf and the slope.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) indicated that if we confine ourselves to the shelf and the slope we will not include salmon. He is right. This would not include swordfish, tuna, and a number of other species that swim along the margin of the continents. In our measures for conservation, in our management of these resources, we should pay close attention to the life cycle of all our fish stocks. Therefore, we should think in terms of territory which is not simply the shelf, not simply the slope, but also areas close to the slope of the continent or continents where great upwellings occur, where ocean currents bring food to the surface, and where many fish populations congregate and feed. Many of the groundfish which are common to the continental shelf, in fact, swim out over the great ocean deeps nearby.
. So in the wise management of those resources we should concern ourselves not simply with the shelf and the slope but with margins beyond that, and our management approach must be that of the geography of the fish and not the topography of the bottom. However, the shelf concept is important because, in a general way although in a somewhat limited way, it describes where 95 per cent of the fish resources spend their lifetime.
I first advocated, in a speech in Boston in 1968, that the continental shelf be the general topographical ambit within which Canada should manage its fish stocks, and within which the coastal nations the world over should endeavour to manage fish resources in the best possible fashion. This because very few fish are found beyond the shelf and the neighbouring waters adjoining the shelf.
I realize that some hon. members from the NDP have advocated limits at the edge of the shelf; they have advocated 200 miles; they have advocated even greater distances at times and have been talking in terms of these extended jurisdictions for a decade or more. They were speaking in those terms in the House. However, they did not have the responsibility of trying to negotiate arrangements with other nations or make sure that those nations observed those limits.
I think that as Canadians we must be doubly conscious of the fact that at least on the Atlantic side of Canada, the
Grand Banks, the vast fishing areas off our east coast, have been fished by many nations for centuries. We cannot unilaterally kick them out. We have been moving in that direction but we have been doing so by negotiation and, I hope, sweet reason rather than the use of gunboats.
When I say "sweet reason" I think that the approach we used, for example, at the world conference sponsored by FAO and convened under our leadership in Vancouver this spring, was that kind of approach. Basically, we have stressed conservation. Conservation was the fundamental idea, the fundamental concept which we wanted to pursue, and our management techniques must be designed to ensure that all stocks are kept at levels consistent with a productive fishing effort.
The term used in the industry is sustained yield. It is well known in the forest industry. It is being practiced increasingly in the world's fishing industries. Sustained yield as a term should be further defined. It does not mean the maximum biological sustained yield; rather it is the maximum economic yield. This is a lower rate of catch. It means less pressure on fish stocks than does the maximum sustained biological yield.
In any case, we have been preaching this doctrine, first, to protect the species from extinction; second, to enhance the incomes of fishermen who are so heavily dependent on the health of the fish stocks and, finally, to make sure that in the longer run Canadians do, in fact, get the maximum economic yield from our vast fish resources.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said some of the right things. He is a compassionate gentleman and I know he is a conscientious man. He was pessimistic on one count, however, and I found that distressing. He was pessimistic about our ability to convince the fishing nations of the world that sound conservation was in their best interests, and that management practices which involved the idea of optimum sustained yield would not carry the day.
We have evidence that these are succeeding. This week in Copenhagen the North Atlantic Fisheries Commission is holding its annual meeting. That meeting comprises 15 nations that fish in the north Atlantic and it has been meeting for close to a quarter of a century. For a long time, it was really a scientists' club. It developed data, it developed ideas, but it was not until the last few years that the idea of converting this data into quotas and into management criteria really caught hold. Indeed, it was only in 1972 when they met in Washington that the message we had been preaching for several years turned up in the form of quotas. The result of that developing consensus among the 15 nations, Canada included, was quotas for several of the major fish species taken in many of the major fishing areas of the north Atlantic.
I think it is important to state that scientists had a maximum input. Their evidence on the state of each stock was taken fully into account. The maximum sustained yield was calculated from that evidence and it was evidence from the international scientific community, not simply from a few fishing nations. The maximum sustained yield, having been set as the maximum catch for the north Atlantic, was then divided between nations and

June 7, 1973

Canada, being a coastal state, got the largest slice of the overall quota, if I may put it that way. Canada got 10 per cent extra for the expansion of its fishery. In fact, we were not able to take up all of the fish allocated to us during the last 12 months. As far as we can determine, all 15 countries lived within their quotas. They did not, in total, take more fish than the scientists indicated could be taken without seriously reducing the stocks. While expanding her catch, Canada still did not in fact take all the fish allocated to her fishermen.
This year we are trying to revise the formula in close consultation with the fishermen and the industry. We hope to get the other 14 nations to agree that in 1973-74 we should be able to take everything we can catch. We will be hard put to take more than the quota allocated to us last year. We seem to have convinced these countries, however, that the coastal state does in fact have a special claim on the resources swimming along its shores, living its life over the continental shelf, over its slope and out into those other waters where the groundfish also feed during part of their lifetime.
One of the fundamental problems that the world fisheries face was largely tackled and overcome toward the end of the middle ages as it concerned agriculture. The great debates over the commons and what would happen to the commons finally resulted in enclosures. Only when land was enclosed and allocated to an owner was it properly managed. Prior to that time, everyone had turned as many sheep, as many cattle, out on the commons as they could. The commons were over-grazed. It was a case of the devil take the hindmost. The stock was in poor shape and, of course, not as many could be maintained under those circumstances as in the enclosed type of agriculture we know today.
This is happening in the world fisheries. Adjoining waters are being divided up so as to conserve their resources. I am not really suggesting that Canada should harvest those resources exclusively, certainly not in the next few decades because there are many species that we do not take yet, although we may begin to take them in time. First of all, we have no taste for them and there is no market on this continent or with the more affluent nations of northern Europe and, second, we do not happen to have the techniques. But where there are resources within these boundaries, which I believe the coastal state should in large measure determine and certainly manage, we should be prepared to give licence under contract or some kind of arrangement to other nations to either come in or to contract with Canadian companies or Canadian fishermen, and fish and process the resources on our shores.
I am optimistic about this because there is a limited supply of fish in the world, certainly in the wild state off the shores of the continent. At the same time, the demand for seafood is mounting steadily and has been for several decades at the rate of 5 per cent a year. The market for fish 15 years from now will be twice as large. As a broad generalization, world fish stocks will not stand much heavier fishing than they are presently exposed to. If the demand is to keep rising and the supply is limited, it is obvious that prices will continue to rise as they have in the last few years, so it is going to pay other countries to enter into arrangements with the coastal states for the
Fisheries
coastal states to do much of the harvesting. However, it must be done under sound management, using the best conservation practices so that fish stocks are there forever in quantities which will permit a maximum economic yield from the resources.
Ten years ago Canada's fishing limit was three miles running close along the coast, and that is what it was during the period that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister. In 1964, legislation was passed to extend the limit to 12 miles so until the early 70's that was our limit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I admit that I could have used better language. Since members on this side of the House invented the term and since fisheries closing lines are a Canadian invention, I should use the same terminology. In any case, the total area enclosed by drawing these base lines and fisheries closing lines around Canada's very extensive coast-the total area, which became in 1971 the exclusive fishing zones of Canada-added up to over 700,000 square miles. I mention that figure, because members often talk about South American countries and their 200-mile limits, and the vast extent of their unilaterally declared fishing zones. Chile's 200-mile limit added roughly 1 million square miles to that country's fishing area,

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
300,000 more than our 700,000 square miles. Brazil's 200-mile territorial sea covers about 1.1 million square miles. By contrast, the United States 12-mile limit, which follows its coastline closely, has added only 131,000 square miles, as compared with our 700,000. The United Kingdoms limits which go out 12 miles added 33,000 square miles compared with our 700,000. Italy's zone includes 39,000 square miles, and so on. But few other countries have extended their fishing limits to the extent we did.
Our extension of exclusive fishing zone limits is a recent happening. Our closing lines are years old. While we draw them to some degree unilaterally, we also entered into negotiations with half a dozen nations for the phasing out of their fishing operations. For example, with respect to the Gulf of St. Lawrence, we now have agreements with all the countries which fish there, and those agreements see an end to the operation of their fishing fleets in our exclusive fishing zones. These zones, as I have mentioned, are very large in extent.
We, among other things, brought to an end a more than 200-year old treaty with France. In a few years fishing vessels from metropolitan France will no longer be coming to the Gulf of St. Lawrence for example. Such countries, as a result of signing agreements for phasing out fishing with Canada, really recognized, for all time, the extent of our exclusive fishing zones as we know them, as they now appear on our maps, as they now appear on the charts of captains responsible for the navigation of fishing vessels owned by other nations that come close to our shores. Those are our limits today.
Many of the fish stocks we have harvested have been taken far out, beyond the Gulf of St. Lawrence, or well outside Queen Charlotte Sound on the west coast. We must be concerned about the total life cycle of the fish, about their lifetime habitat, which includes the shelf and the slope as well as those adjoining waters of the ocean which supply great quantities of food for our fish stocks, and which are therefore important to their management. I am speaking of a biological map, if I may call it that. That is the area in which these wild living things spend their lifetime, and is the area within which we have to manage fish stocks. The approach we must take, in my view, at the next Law of the Sea Conference, is that we must endeavour, first, to conserve these stocks and, second, that as we are the coastal state most closely involved, with the greatest concern and interest, that the responsibility should rest with us. That is a principle which should operate around the world, with all coastal states having that responsibility. It should not be exercised to the total exclusion of other nations, because at times, there will be a surplus for harvest and because other nations will have an appetite for many of the fish which the coastal state would not ordinarily take for its own use.
I am optimistic about the future of our fishery, even though there has been great pressure from foreign fleets off our shores. This optimism is shared by our industry. A large number of fishing vessels are being built at the present time. Confining my comments to the Atlantic coast, the total value of vessels under construction is about $18 million, of which roughly $5 million is for small boats in the 35 to 75 foot category and $13 million for those in the bigger trawler category. Plans have been announced
for next year. They see a total of $46 million allocated, of which $16 million is for boats from 35 feet to 75 feet in length, and $30 million for large trawlers over 75 feet in length.
This is by far the biggest fishing vessel building program this country has ever seen. I cannot believe that our fishermen are wrong, that the fishing companies are wrong or that the fishing industry does not know what it is doing. They have some faith in ICNAF. They have some faith in our ability to manage our fish out to the edge of the continental shelf and beyond. It acknowledges our recent achievement in establishing an inside track position for the coastal state and it knows, as well, and this has been reported to the Fisheries Committee by representatives from the fisheries service and of the Department of External Affairs, that the consensus developed among the members of the United Nations is that the coastal state must have a major say over its coastal resources. There is a consensus about extending limits 200 miles seaward.
I prefer always to talk in terms of conservation in areas where the fish live and over which they travel as well as into the areas through which they travel during their lifetime. Any figure regarding limits, whether it be a three-mile limit, 12-mile limit or 200-mile limit, I find arbitrary.
According to my reading, the large majority of fishing nations, indeed, of the underdeveloped and other nations of the world which will be going to the Law of the Sea Conference, will have made up their minds and opt for the 200-mile limit. As it happens, 200 miles roughly covers our eastern shelf and slope and most productive near-by waters, with the exception of the Flemish gap; the 200-mile limit, as a generalization, would be a lot better from our point of view than a 12-mile limit or a 50-mile limit. Certainly, I would be surprised if Canada were to vote contrary to a resolution which advocates 200 miles and has built into it the philosophy of sound conservation and good management.
There are several tough questions which we may have to face in the not too distant future. One relates to port closures. This prickly question and has come up before. We used it on the west coast to force the Russians to talk to us about over-fishing off the west coast. We may have to use that kind of leverage on the east coast. I hope not. We are studying the effects on the merchants in our ports of invoking emergency measures of this kind. There are many other issues that have to be faced in detail.
The least discussed and potentially most controversial is that relating to joint ventures with other countries with large populations and rising standard of living, countries prepared, eventually, to pay almost any price for fish. Faced with a likely 200-mile limit, or some such limit, they want, somehow, to get a corner on production which may involve possibly a number of coastal states.
I know the Japanese have been making inquiries. I know that several companies in this country have held discussions with the West Germans and Japanese on joint ventures, under which Canadians would do the fishing in Canadian-owned vessels, and Canadians would do the processing in Canadian-owned plants, but the production would be tailored for certain foreign markets. The joint

June 7, 1973	COMMONS DEBATES	4539
venture would be arranged in such a way that the country putting up, say, 50 per cent of the capital or 50 per cent of the working inventory would have a claim on the supply of fish over a period of years. This verges on foreign ownership. It raises the question as to how long these contracts or agreements should be allowed to run. But they are compatible with the idea of coastal states having control over the living resources off their coasts and responsibility for the wise management of these resources, more than some other arrangements we could enter into. They are far better than the first come first served arrangements, if I can call them arrangements, which now exist off our shores.
As I say, we are developing a system of quotas in the North Atlantic, but we need to improve them. We need to expand our own effort and increase our Canadian take. We should be doing the catching because we are far more efficient than foreigners are. We are two or three times as efficient as the Russians with their big trawlers. Processing on shore is much more economic than on ships at sea. When the vessels only have to go a few miles, or at the most 200 or 300 miles from shore, obviously their travel time and expenses for fuel and so on are much less than those of nations which have to send their fleets half way around the world. The economics are in favour of the coastal state doing the fishing and the processing as well.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to an article in the London Economist which I have not read. It indicated to me that the United Kingdom was in the process of throwing up its hands and suggested that it should exploit its own shelf or 200 miles or some such concept and buy its extra fish abroad rather than to fish close to countries with a coastal fishery. They should get into joint ventures of the type I already envisaged. I can imagine the United Kingdom getting into joint ventures, not only with Canadians, but with other countries, developed and underdeveloped in Africa, South America and around the world.

I agree that is what it confers. However, we must remember that by a very short margin Canada missed obtaining the 12 mile limit for which the minister is claiming sole responsibility. I say this only to get party lines straight at this particular stage.
Having said that, I wish to turn to those areas of the problem on which I will base my remarks. I have, of course, a vested interest in this debate. I am proud to have that vested interest and I intend to represent it fully here. In my area there are deep-sea fishermen, inshore fishermen and sports fishermen. I wonder whether the present government is doing enough to sustain, maintain and expand those enterprises which are so much a part of Canada's heritage. We rely on the living resources of the sea for our way of life and our food. I maintain that not enough is done for that interest. The government claims it has great plans afoot but relating their comments to their actions, one is permitted to wonder and be confused.
I propose to deal with only two aspects because of the limited time allotted to me; first, the fishing safeguards and, if time permits, pollutions safeguards which are, of course, closely inter-related with our fishing safeguards.
As far as the fishing safeguards are concerned, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) recently talked bravely about going out 200 miles. He said, and I quote:
We will go, flat out, for an exclusive fishing zone which will include the fringes of our Continental Shelf ... Whenever our continental margin reaches out more than two-hundred miles from shore, it is the continental margin which will form our fishing limit-
He said more along these lines, all of it in the context of exclusive fishing rights. Those were brave words. I notice that recently he has toned down these claims a bit and is now only talking in terms of management. This brings me to a point I made even before hearing the minister, namely, that I find claims of this sort hardly credible. They are even less credible now because he has backed off from that claim to a large, exclusive fishing area. The map which the minister circulated along with the text of his comments on that particular occasion bravely extolled the nationalistic and sovereign delights of these vast claims, but is this truly credible? Is this claim of his one that, through the actions or plans of his government, he can substantiate in practical or even theoretical terms?
In a debate last February, I referred to the size of Canada's coast guard. On the basis of the latest statistics I could find, May 1972, I stated that we had some 32 vessels in Canada's coast guard designated as patrol vessels. Let us say we have 40 today. That is being most generous.

The minister spoke just now, and I will accept his figures, that the extension of our fishing limits covered some 700,000 square miles. Going further, I was doing a bit of calculating and I arrived at a figure of about 2 million extra square miles to be patrolled by some 120 vessels. I find this is asking a good deal of crews, particularly when we cannot find them as indicated by the fact the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) had to lay up some of our vessels because he cannot man them. There is nothing in the program of the government which encourages the native heritage of Canada, which is going to sea. We cannot find mariners for our naval vessels and we are doing everything to discourage our fishermen. This clearly indicates how non-credible is the minister and the policies he is advocating.
Let us look at the situation in a nother light. What are the officials who advise the government saying about exclusive fishing rights? Not long ago in a committee we heard a lengthy statement on territorial sea matters by one of the government's most knowledgeable and practised advisers. After dealing with the rights of coastal states to the continental shelf, and even to the continental margin, a matter which for many purposes was settled by international convention in 1968, this specialist said:

All in all, the government is not doing enough to protect our fisheries, or to encourage our youth to garner the harvest that is theirs. It is not doing enough to encourage fishermen to go to sea, or to build a viable coastguard. It shames me to hear that when there is an accident off our shores the United States Coastguard is called in to pick up survivors. Why does Canada not have a coastguard worthy of the name? We do not have sufficient fisheries patrolmen, either. Our tradition as seamen is not being upheld.
This is not all. We are faced with the knotty problem of split or undecided jurisdiction in the area of maritime control. We have been told here and there in the question period and in committee about the hopes of the fisheries department to wrest control of harbours from transport and to get public works to do the building and maintenance of the facilities within the harbours. This I consider to be business management run wild. Divide and misrule, I call it.
Then, the defence department gets into the act. Listen to this. In the course of questioning the Minister of National Defence only two weeks ago, on May 22, we went into the question of the environmental protection and surveillance responsibilities allotted to our naval and air forces. As reported at page 29 and 30 of the minutes of the 13th meeting of the Committee on External Affairs and Defence, we heard the deputy minister of national defence outlining the problems of multiple jurisdiction or coordinated command. All we got out of that discussion was

that a complex study of this question had been undertaken but because the inquiry would involve matters touching on security it could not be made public. This suggests to me that we are still nowhere near determining, in a crisis, which authority goes to sea and for what purpose. Is it a fisheries patrol vessel, is it a coastguard, is it a naval vessel or is it an RCMP vessel? The fisheries and environment people and the coastguard are clamouring for definitions, but the government has not provided any of the answers. So, there we are.
