speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which has just been introduced in the House bears on an issue which for a very long time, in fact since the very beginning of Canada, has been of great significance for the economic life and the welfare of the population. Besides being one of the first resources to be developed near the North American coasts, fishing has long been one of the most sturdy supports for our dawning economy. Since our fishing resources are also at the limits of our country, they have brought us into contact with our next-door neighbours and many other countries, and that has rapidly led us to conduct, in that field, more and more extensive activities and assume our own responsibilities. Every member recalls, for example, that the first treaty concluded and signed by Canadians was a convention concerning halibut fishing and our bilateral relations with the United States of America.
In a way, it is fair to say that the situation has not changed much, because fisheries remain a very important area of our national and international activities and that, once again, we must consider how Canada can turn to the best account the biological resources along our coasts and how to defend our interests in the light of new circumstances prevailing in the world today. So, Mr. Speaker, I should like to describe briefly the present situation concerning the matter of national jurisdiction over maritime fishing.
We will recall that for centuries fishing was part and parcel of the concept of the freedom of the sea, and that consequently the fishermen of the whole world could, without restraint, give free course to their talent and their boldness on all the seas of the world. It is only in recent years that we have realized that this total freedom could lead to serious impoverishment and in some cases to complete extinction of biological resources of the sea and that it became imperative to set up new rules if we wanted to preserve those important natural resources.
As the hon. Minister of Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) recalled earlier, Canada was one of the very first countries to propose, in 1958 and 1960 at the Geneva Law of the Sea Conference, that beyond the traditional three-mile territorial sea it was advisable that coastal states should obtain certain rights over a wider area for the exploitation of their resources.
As early as 1964, Canada set up a nine-mile fishing zone beyond the three-mile territorial sea and thus contributed to develop a new concept to guarantee better control over fishing by coastal states.
In 1970, this control was enlarged to even more important areas by extending the territorial waterline to 12 miles and creating exclusive fishing zones in the gulf of the St. Lawrence, Fundy bay, Dixon entrance, Hecate's Strait and Queen Charlotte Strait.

Those efforts have already brought us important benefits but our offshore fisheries are still subject under international law to a freedom which does not seem to us adequate. We believe that the Great Banks of Newfoundland for instance which for four centuries have attracted fishermen from all over the world, must from now on be governed by new regulations, new concepts. Obviously, the matter does not come under the exclusive jurisdiction of Canada and as is the case in all the seas of the world, fishing must be submitted to regulations universally recognized and applicable to everyone. These concerns are, of course, shared by most states of the world and this is why studies were undertaken under the auspices of the United Nations to develop adequate solutions to this problem.
The United Nations sea bed committee who is now preparing the third law of the Sea Conference is developing a fisheries system that will allow hopefully a better use and conservation of biological resources of the sea. it should be noted that in the same time, this committee also works on problems that have a direct impact on fisheries such as defining the rights of coastal states on the continental shelf and the rights and duties of those states with regard to prevention of pollution. Canada is no doubt one of the countries which were most actively involved in these studies and which contributed most to the development of an almost general agreement not only on the goals to be reached but also on the approach most likely to ensure the success of the operation.
Being aware of the importance of fishing in some areas of our country-including the constituency of Matane which I have the honour to represent-and, in a wider sense, for the whole of Canada, but realizing-which I feel is the most important-the interdependency of all nations of the world, we wish to emphasize that besides being tinted with economic egotism our policy but would above all take into account the primary importance that must be given to this vital resource and its conservation, it might therefore have been easier, but much too simplistic, to propose to the community of nations that they simply share the oceans and their resources and draw more or less arbitrary off-shore limits. Instead, we have decided that the only defensible position under these circumstances, was to treat fishing in a functional way, taking into account not only the geography and the very nature of the various species, but also the related economic and social factors and the necessity to maintain rational control over these activities. We must be delighted that that functional approach now seems to be meeting the acceptance of most countries. Indeed, when considering the concepts put forward by some countries in the context of the law of the sea, like those of the off-shore sea and the economic zone, one can only conclude that that reflects in different ways a practical implementation of that functional policy. Once again I must point out that Canada has been innovative when establishing three years ago its exclusive fishing zones where are already found in fact the main elements of the proposals now under serious consideration by the United Nations, that is the establishment within a certain zone of the rights and privileges in favour of coastal states, in connection with fishing resources, continental shelf resources and the prevention of sea pollution.
June 7, 1973	______________COMMONS
As you know we already have this jurisdiction over the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the Bay of Fundy, Hecate Straight, Dixon Entrance and Queen Charlotte Sound.
This policy has a double objective: First, it is obvious that those guidelines should lead to a workable system that should ensure our fishermen and the Canadian people the protection required for the maximum exploitation and conservation of our biological resources. On the other hand, the interests of the international community should obviously be taken into account and it would be a mistake to ignore the human and political context we are living in and to deny to others rights obtained through tradition or which are theirs by the very nature of things. Many countries which are not endowed as we are and which cannot find near their coasts the fish resources required for their survival and trade have been, for years, intensively exploiting the biological resources of all the oceans and, in several cases, quite far out from their own coastal regions. Quite naturally the coastal nations have responded to this mass intrusion of foreign fishing fleets over banks situated near their territories. In view of the modern technology now used by those fleets it became obvious that pure and simple competition between coastal nations and remote fishing nations would have quickly entailed the loss of major resources. No one would have won anything in the long run. It goes without saying that a solution should be found to this confrontation and that we must urgently reconcile the views and interests of all nations involved.
The current negotiations should therefore take into account the opposition of certain very important countries which do not agree with coastal states extending their jurisdiction over large regions. An ideal policy consisting in a coastal state assuming outright control over all resources off its shores would be hardly negociable. It is also obvious that purely and simply maintaining the traditional fishing freedom would not constitute an element of fruitful negotiations either.
Therefore, what is to be done? Considering the positions developed by our natural allies in that field, namely those coastal states that are concerned above all with the resources adjacent to their shores, one realizes that a good number of them chose to secure rights and privileges over a zone up to 200 miles off-shore. As things are now, one can say that those states now represent a majority within the international community. But the kind of rights and privileges to be enjoyed by the coastal state over such a zone have yet to be defined. Some would like those rights to be exclusive, which would entail of course the automatic exclusion of fishermen from other states over large sea areas. Now very few states can say they are able to fish all the resources of those areas. Setting aside for themselves the exclusive right to such resources would be neither practical nor reasonable, given the protein needs throughout the world especially in the underdeveloped countries.
On the basis of scientific statistics, the Canadian government on the one hand deems essential that the coastal state keep for itself the exclusive administration of fishing resources and, on the other hand, firmly believes that the coastal state, while setting aside for itself a preferential share of the production, must allow other states to use the surplus of such resources that it cannot or does not want
DEBATES	4543
Fisheries
to take itself. Obviously, the coastal state must have all the necessary latitude to determine, on its own, what share it has coming to it, and to regulate the activity of other countries so that its own activity will not result in a serious decrease or the complete destruction of its stocks.
The question of knowing whether the rights of coastal states will be exclusive, totally or only partly, still remains to be decided at the next Law of the Sea Conference, but there is another equally important matter to which I alluded a few moments ago and which is particularly important to Canada, namely, the question of the limit of the jurisdiction to be exercised by the coastal state. I said that there is a tendency now to grant the coastal state some jurisdiction over fisheries up to 200 miles. Of course, in the case of most countries that distance covers the entirety of so-called coastal species since in most cases the continental shelf of those countries where those species live does not extend beyond 200 miles. However, the situation is entirely different in the case of the East Coast of Canada where the continental shelf of Newfoundland extends beyond 400 miles. On the same scientific grounds that led us to adopt a functional policy, it was normal for Canada to claim rights over that whole area, that is to say up to the limits of the continental shelf since that is where fish is found. It would be foolish to suggest that a state can manage, conserve and exploit adequately stocks lying within an arbitrary limit of 200 miles, without taking into account the elements of those stocks to be found in adjacent areas. A single stock must therefore come under one regulation because, otherwise, the effect of uncontrolled activity in one part would of course be disastrous for the other part of the stock. That is the position Canada defended and continues to defend because we think it is the only defendible position if a rational plan is to be established with respect to coastal fisheries.
Up to now, Mr. Speaker, I have only referred to the so-called coastal species, those which are found mainly on the continental shelf and which depend upon it for their conservation and development. Needless to say, the Canadian government was also concerned with other species of fish, some of which are of prime importance to Canada. I refer in particular to anadromous species, such as salmon. We took the stand, and we intend to maintain it, that salmon should be restricted, wherever it may be found, to the fishermen of the state where it was spawned. Without the large amounts of money and numerous efforts devoted to the reproduction of this species by the state where it is spawned, salmon could not exist, but of course, it is quite natural for it to happen to be, at some time or other, in territorial waters other than those of its country of origin. In such circumstances, interceptions are inevitable, and that problem naturally lends itself to bilateral solutions. Otherwise, there is no doubt that only the state of spawning should be entitled to catch this species.
Non-migrant species which live on the continental shelf are already covered by the Continental Shelf Convention of 1958, which Canada signed, the sovereign rights of coastal states.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that this government has advocated the most appropriate policy to guarantee Canadian fishermen all the necessary protection for the

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
development of their industry, and to ensure that their individual welfare and their contribution to national welfare continue to improve. A policy based exclusively on sovereignty concepts would only emphasize the disputes which already take place amongst some nations of the world. We developed legislation and regulations to protect our fisheries, but we have also reached agreements with given countries whenever necessary. We will continue to assert our rights at the international level, but we will also endeavour to ensure that proper consideration is given to the legitimate interests of other States and the international community as a whole.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to rise to take part in this debate to support the motion presented this afternoon by my leader dealing with the principle that Canada and other coastal states own the fisheries resources on and over their respective continental shelves and slopes, that the management of these fisheries resources is the responsibility of the coastal state and that other states may only fish such resources with the permission of the coastal state. I naturally support that motion.
Before I become too involved, I should like to take exception to the remarks made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) in the course of his speech in New Brunswick last week, because I am sure the minister must be aware of the position taken by our party in this matter on September 22, 1972 at a meeting of our Atlantic caucus in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island. At that time our party stated its position with regard to our marine resources. I should like to read into the record a part of the release which came from that conference concerning our marine resources. It reads:
.. . under this new department, launch a new, aggressive program to extend Canada's managerial control to the extremities of its continental shelf, for conservation and management of its marine resources;
I think the minister must have been aware of that resolution. Certainly, the people of Atlantic Canada were well aware of it. I am at a loss to understand why he would so deliberately try to misinterpret the views of our party and or our members in respect of our position regarding the continental shelf. I am rather surprised also to see the tug-of-war which obviously is taking place between certain members of the government.
The Minister of Fisheries in his speech at St. Andrews mentioned the continental shelf and came out with a program whereby we would go all out or flat out for exclusive fishing rights including the fringes of the continental shelf. However, a few days later, I believe on Monday, May 28, the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) introduced a motion in this House under Standing Order 43 in which he called upon the House to stand behind that principle. The motion was not allowed unanimous consent. I understand the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) is one of the members who refused this unanimous consent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
This did not surprise me, and I am sure it did not surprise most people in Atlantic Canada, because we know where the Secretary of State for External Affairs stands when it comes to fishing. As a matter of fact in 1953, in a speech, the minister stated that the fishery represents poverty and should be allowed to die. This is a statement made by the man who now occupies the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs. He outlined his attitude toward the fishing industry and the fact that it represented poverty and should be allowed to die. I am concerned that if a tug-of-war is in the making our Minister of Fisheries, as good as his intentions are, in all likelihood will lose the war because we have seen the influence the Secretary of State for External Affairs can exercise on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and we have seen how well he can represent the views of his Bay Street constituents in respect of policies made by the Prime Minister and this government.
I feel that if there is to be a battle between the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Atlantic area and indeed Canada, could very well come out on the wrong end of the stick. If that should happen, it would be extremely regrettable because we all know that our fish stocks are seriously declining to a point where it is now almost uneconomic to fish. Surely, if the present situation is allowed to prevail much longer it will be uneconomic to fish and a large segment of our population will be deprived of an opportunity to derive a livelihood from that industry. I make that statement in the light of figures which were released to the effect that in 1971 our catches represented, I believe, two and a half billion pounds. This figure was reduced in 1972 by almost 300 million pounds, despite the fact that the capability of our fishing fleets had increased due to improved technology, improved gear and so on.
This situation, of course, is all the more alarming in Atlantic Canada because we find that approximately 75 per cent of all the fish caught in Canada come from the Atlantic area. This is a rather shameful situation. I believe it is a very serious indictment of the present government which has allowed this situation to continue and worsen. We find that in respect of the Atlantic area-I have said this before in committee and in the House-there seems to be a complete and utter indifference to the fishing industry. We find that the government is totally insensitive to the needs of the area in respect of harbour and marine facilities. I am sure the records of the Committee on Public Works and the sub-committee on public works in respect of small craft harbours contain some very interesting and very alarming statistics which reflect the attitude of this government toward the fishing industry, particularly in Atlantic Canada.
We find that the expenditure on public works, such as harbour and wharf facilities, this year is to be 25 per cent of what it was in 1951. These are not my figures but rather are figures that were quoted at the meeting of the subcommittee to which I have just referred by highly placed officials of the Department of Public Works. We find, according to their testimony before the committee, that this year it would cost approximately $30 million to properly maintain and service our facilities in Atlantic Canada while in fact they are this year spending I believe a little over $15 million. I think this is pretty indicative of the

attitude of the present government in respect of the fishing industry, particularly in Atlantic Canada. It is a very alarming fact when we realize that so many of our people depend on the fishing industry for a livelihood.
Earlier I mentioned my views in respect of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the fact that I believe the gentleman in question has no compassion whatever for the fishermen, and no optimism in respect of the fishing industry. I think that attitude has been reflected in the statement the minister made in 1953 when he referred to the fishing industry as representing poverty. He no doubt made that statement in view of the fact that according to official statistics the fishing industry accounts for less than 2 per cent of the gross national product of Canada. I think, therefore, it has become a political question.
The question, of course, is: why should we cater to the people involved in the fishing industry? Why should we cater to the regions in Canada where the fishing industry is important, when it represents such a small percentage of our gross national product? That question is very misleading in that the fishing industry represents much more than the reported 2 per cent. In fact, according to an economist with the Memorial University in Newfoundland, a man who has spent considerable time studying the effects of the fishing industry in Canada as a whole, the fishing industry is seventh in importance among all Canadian industries. When one realizes that a number of service industries are connected with the fishing industry, employing a number of people who derive a living from the fishing industry but yet never go out to the sea to fish, one cannot help but be surprised at the fact that so little attention has been paid to it by the government, and in particular by the Minister of Fisheries.
In my riding, fishing plays a very important part in our economy. There are communities in my riding where the fishing industry is all important and if the fishing industry were to die, the community would die. In the province of Newfoundland which I represent, if the fishing industry were to fail, the economy of our whole province would be shattered to such an extent that I doubt we could survive economically. That is why those of us in particular who represent Newfoundland are so anxious that action be taken immediately to adopt a sane approach to the management and control of our marine resources.
Of course, it is laughable to observe the government's attitude with regard to surveillance and control. I was amused the other day when in the House we were questioning the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and trying to impress upon him the need to make the four destroyers to which reference had been made available to the Department of Fisheries, rather than mothballing them, so that a proper job of patrolling our coastal waters could be made to protect our fishermen. The minister's reply was that he was quite satisfied we were doing a good job of patrolling our waters. If he were to tell that to the fishermen in my riding, I am sure he would get a laugh out of them.
It is obvious to all of us, particularly to the people who are affected, that this government is not doing its duty in properly patrolling our waters and protecting our fisher-
Fisheries
men from the ravaging of foreign fishing ships. Not only do these foreign fishermen rob our fish stocks and contribute to the depletion of our marine resources, but in the process in many cases they destroy the fishing gear of our fishermen. Then, they just thumb their noses at our fishermen and fade out into the sunset, not giving a thought to paying any compensation and with no respect for authority and law. This is a sad situation because fishing gear is vital to the operation of fishermen. Without it, they cannot fish. In many cases, fishing gear represents a substantial sum of money, certainly an amount which fishermen should not be expected to forfeit as the result of actions by foreign fishing fleets.
One alarming effect of the activities of foreign fishing vessels is that, for years now, we have noted an abrupt decline in our fish stocks. For the past number of years we have found that the catches of our fishermen were seriously declining. Yet, we have been prodding this government, and particularly the Minister of Fisheries, to try to bring about some method of control and management of our marine resources. However, I am afraid that our pleas have fallen on deaf ears, and very little action has been taken by him to protect our fish stocks. He has imposed other regulations on the advice of his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs with respect to seals. There are times, it seems, when the minister is quite willing, indeed anxious, to impose certain regulations. This is so often the case that at times we think perhaps he should be called minister of the environment, fish restrictions and regulations. Yet, when it comes to protecting that all important species, our groundfish, he seems unwilling to take any action that would have the effect of staving off the day when the extinction of this species would occur.
We have seen the minister take steps to curb the killing of baby seals. We all realize that it is not a pretty sight to see animals being killed. Yet, those of us in Atlantic Canada continue to hold very strong views concerning the wisdom of the minister's regulation with respect to that animal. We know how it came about. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and our ambassadors in foreign countries could not stand the thought of being badgered by the sob sisters of SPCA at their cocktail parties. Imagine that, they could not go to a cocktail party in European capitals or in New York without being approached by some lady wearing her mink stole and her kid gloves who, after having eaten a full sized meal of calves' liver and bacon, would come up to them and make objections to the killing of baby seals. Of course, the Secretary of State for External Affairs could not allow his staff to be harassed by such people, and consequently the Minister of Fisheries agreed to impose these restrictions, the effect of which was to pretty well ruin our sealing industry.
We have seen the minister impose other regulations with regard to whales, swordfish and salmon. This seems to be a government that is more concerned with imposing regulations on our own people, on our own fishermen, restricting their area of activity, than with talking sternly to the Russians, the Cubans, the French, the Spaniards, the East Germans and the Portuguese. You name them and they are there. What we want is a minister of fisheries, a government, and a secretary of state for external affairs who would be prepared to take off their gloves, if

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
they have to, and tell these people that fish in our waters belong to this country and that they can fish them only by Canada's leave and licence.

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting motion. The minister has already said that he can find little to disagree with in the motion except for the fact that it does not go far enough.
There are certain points in the motion which interest me. It reads:
That this House accepts the principle that Canada and other coastal states own the fishery resources on and over their respective continental shelves and slopes.
In other words, what it is really saying is that basically the opposition is adopting the same position as this government will be taking at the Law of the Sea conference. Yet, if it is that, on the one hand, members of the opposition are saying that basically they agree with the position that Canada will be taking at the Law of the Sea conference and, on the other hand, they are expressing pessimism regarding whether in fact this position can be improved. They say it is a good position to take, but can we actually do it?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext: We are not accepting that position, my friend. Tell the House the truth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext: You people have thrown cold water on ICNAF and on the Law of the Sea conference. The only alternative, then, is gunboat diplomacy. I think the opposition should come out clearly and say whether they are in favour of our ships firing on vessels of foreign nations and having them fire back on our ships.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
I had better classes when I was teaching, I can tell you that; they were much more orderly.
I think the Conservative party should come out quite clearly and say whether they are in favour of ships firing on other ships and precipitating an international incident. There are two alternatives; either gunboat diplomacy or "walk softly, and carry a big stick," in the words of Teddy Roosevelt. I think it should be clearly stated which of the two alternatives the opposition favours.
In many ways, the fishing industry in this country is in good shape at the present time. There are many indications of this. We have talked about the federal contribution to shipbuilding in the Atlantic provinces. In Newfoundland alone this means a federal contribution, for 1973-74, through a 50 per cent construction subsidy of $5 million. In addition there is the possibility of construction at the Marystown shipyard of ten 65-foot, steel, multipurpose units with a capacity of landing another seven million pounds. This represents jobs for 305 men for one full year. When in operation these ships will provide continuing employment for 272 crew members on a year-round basis. This contribution to shipbuilding is important to the fisheries as well.
There are other indications that in general terms the industry is in good shape. Fish prices have increased. For

instance, cod blocks have risen from 21 cents per pound in 1969 to 62 cents per pound in 1973. The Salt Fish Corporation, even though cold water was thrown on it in committee by members from Nova Scotia, has put money in the pockets of fishermen. Choice, light-salted cod was selling for $27 per quintal in 1969; it is now selling for $49. It is true that in the last couple of years landings have gone down, but from 1953 to 1971 landings per fisherman increased from 29,000 pounds to 45,000 pounds. The available statistics show that in the last two or three years there has been a reduction, but looking at the broad picture it is evident that landings have in fact increased.
The position we are taking at the Law of the Sea Conference is increasingly geared toward improving the fisheries in this country. I want to speak particularly about the Atlantic area, which I represent and which is very much concerned with the fisheries. As a matter of fact, my province of Newfoundland has been historically and traditionally dependent upon the fishery to provide a living for its people, and I am sure it will continue to depend upon the fishery as a prime source of income in its economy.
The two major themes of this government are national unity and the elimination of regional disparity. We have already shown that the government is interested in improving the economy of the Atlantic area to the point that it is self-supporting. As I see it, our position at the Law of the Sea Conference is fulfilling that aim. If we can ensure increased earnings for our inshore fishermen, there will be less need to find alternative employment for them; in other words, DREE need not provide as many alternatives to jobs in the fishing industry if we concentrate our efforts on that industry.
One issue covered at the Law of the Sea Conference is that of control to the end of the continental shelf. If I understand the motion correctly, this is what it calls for. Our position at the conference seeks control to the end of the continental shelf whether it be 200 or 400 miles and, indeed, to the bottom of the continental slope. This is very important because there is a danger of depletion of stocks and only the host nation could have adequate control over those stocks. First of all, we must make sure that we have adequate stocks from which our fishermen can draw.
I was pleased with the appointment of Dr. Arthur May to the marine biology laboratory in St. John's. For some years he has given valuable aid to Canada at Law of the Sea conferences and I am sure that his knowledge will be valuable to the province in carrying out adequate research programs. It is not as easy to do research beneath the surface of the ocean as it is above the surface of the ground; it is not as easy to count fish as it is to count trees, and you cannot predict the same kind of maximum sustained yield in the water as you can on land. But we must go as close to it as we can.
Another point is that, as the host nation, we must have a preferential share in our fisheries' resources. This means that we should be able to fish to the limit of our resources. If we can establish such a policy, our next important point is to make sure that we have the capability with which to carry it out. The minister pointed out that we have not been fishing up to our established quota. If we can achieve control over the continental shelf and ensure preferential
June 7, 1973

fishing rights, our next job is to make sure that our people have adequate technology to enable them to take those stocks. We must not emphasize, as this motion does, limits to the exclusion of facilities; we must view both aspects in context. It is one thing to set a limit and control stocks, to have maximum sustained yield and quotas; but we must also ensure that we have the proper facilities, inshore and offshore, to harvest that yield. This means improvements in technology. I have already pointed out that the government has been putting money into ships and gear; it is subsidizing these areas of the industry in order to help fishermen take more of the resources which, of course, means more money in their pockets.
We have discussed a small craft harbours program in various ways, and at length. There is no point in having quotas and controls if fishermen do not have the facilities with which to reap the proper harvest. We must ensure that breakwaters and other fishing facilities are in good shape, that boats are protected and able to harvest the resources properly. We must bear in mind the program announced recently whereby the department would provide a subsidy for freezing and chilling facilities in small craft harbours throughout Canada. This is important because usually a great deal of the catch is lost due to deterioration.
We must be careful, too, that while we are improving the facilities we improve the infrastructure-water supply, housing and all other facilities. I would like to see many of the OFY, LIP and other programs which have been up to now on an ad hoc basis put on an ongoing, comprehensive basis so that communities can plan ahead and thus make sure that the infrastructure is improved. I would like to see an ongoing program of winter works in connection with our small craft fishing harbours.
In a committee meeting recently my colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Rooney) mentioned the effect that unemployment insurance has in encouraging people to leave the inshore fishery. It has been pointed out that the inshore fishery is possibly the most economical of our fisheries because it is less capital-intensive and therefore brings greater return to individual fishermen. We must make improvements in the unemployment insurance program as it applies to fishermen if we are to ensure that they remain inshore fishermen.
Proposals are already under way, through the proper authorities, to bring about necessary changes in unemployment insurance for fishermen. The only alternative would be some sort of catch insurance or, if I may put it another way, we must ensure a guaranteed annual income for firshermen. The form that this help is to take, whether it be unemployment insurance, catch insurance or any other form, is really a matter for debate and for the government to decide. We must ensure that there is some sort of guaranteed annual income for our fishermen. The other point that came up in our committee meetings recently had to do with greater communication with those in policy-making positions. Indeed, we must provide in future for more input from fishermen at the lower level.
All this, Mr. Speaker, is very important in view of the fact that we have a food problem in the world. We recently
Fisheries
debated in this House the rising cost of food. Only a small percentage of the world's food comes from the sea. In future a great deal more of its food will come from the sea. This means that we must place greater emphasis on the fisheries and emphasize greater returns for our fishermen.
Naturally, I am very concerned about the northeast coast of Newfoundland, that part of my riding which is almost wholly dependent upon the fishery. In a year such as this, when ice conditions have been bad, our fishermen have no income to fall back on. Many have been without income since the middle of March. We all hope that the fall fishing will be good. When the ice has been bad at the beginning of a year it is said that the fall fishery will be good. In the meantime we must provide some form of income for our fishermen.

speechtext: How will you do it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
There are at the present time proposals before the government to do this very thing. I have tried to show that the government has increased its spending on the fishery and I have tried to indicate the areas in which it has done that. I have also tried to indicate some of the problems which remain, which some hon. members have tried to discuss within the context of the motion before the House.
Really, what I am trying to say is this; the first thing we must be concerned about is stocks off-our shores. We must improve our technology to ensure greater returns for our fishermen. We must try to improve market prices. We have done this. We must ensure that with improved market prices all the profits do not remain in the hands of the middleman but that the price paid to the fisherman is improved. We must continue to improve facilities in small craft fishing harbours. Finally, we must attempt to provide a guaranteed annual income of some kind for our fishermen.
The position as set out in the motion varies little from the position of the government. However, if we approach this matter from the point of view of the motion alone we will find it is not enough. We should not consider the motion out of context; I think we must be concerned about the broad spectrum of our fisheries' problems.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable pleasure that I rise to participate in this debate for it provides me with an opportunity to place before the House some of the problems faced by our own fishermen and those engaged in the fish processing industry. Seldom in our history have the people of Atlantic Canada been more concerned over the future of the fishing industry, and they cannot help but question the federal government's role and its future development policy as it concerns this industry. The previous speaker, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Romp-

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
key), made some comment about the healthy aspect of the industry. Although I do not wish to engage in any long controversy with him, I suggest that he read the annual report put out by Environment Canada in which he will find these words:
Canadian landings of fish and shellfish in 1971 amounted to 2.5 billion pounds, 6 per cent less than 1970 and 12 per cent less than the peak year of 1968. The total value to Canadian fishermen at $190.7 million was, however, only 1 per cent lower than in 1970.
On the Atlantic coast, total landings have been declining since the peak in 1968.
I could go on, but I think that is sufficient to show what is happening in Atlantic Canada. The fishing industry is vitally important to Atlantic Canada and it is especially important to Nova Scotia where the landed value last year of all species brought our fishermen a total of approximately $60 million. These species had a market value of approximately double this figure. However, this amount when distributed among our offshore and inshore fishermen still leaves them with an income far below the national average. This situation does little to encourage young men to consider fishing as a vocation. This, I submit, is unfortunate and is a situation which must be changed, and changed very quickly, if the fishing industry is to take its rightful place in Canada's over-all development.
In recent years it would appear that our fishermen and their activities have received a very low priority rating from this government. This fact was recently highlighted when fishermen from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and Quebec appeared before the subcommittee on public works, where all of them without exception deplored the lack of consideration given their requests, as presented by petition through their Members of Parliament, for improved wharves, skid-ways, dredging and breakwaters.
It is utter nonsense for the government to say that it has not been alerted to the fishermen's needs, for in my own constituency the file is fat with copies of petitions forwarded to the government in support of fishermen's requests. The file from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) is equally fat; his communications state that the requests of the fishermen have been noted but no action can be taken at the present time due to shortage of funds. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what is the real reason behind the lack of action on these requests. I wonder why these people, whose requests are so small and reasonable, are denied assistance in order that they may earn a livelihood and add to the gross national product and to our economy. Why were these requests denied while at the same time this government made available millions of dollars in the form of grants, which in some cases do little for society and often are highly questionable?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) cannot boast about a $445 million surplus for the financial year ending March 31, 1973, and at the same time ask us to make any sense whatever out of the statement of the Minister of Public Works that he cannot provide funds for skidways and wharves because there is no money available. You simply cannot have it both ways. And to judge from discussions I have had with fishermen, they are not being fooled by the manner in which the government is attempting to fog the issue. Surely the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) must be aware of these
situations, and surely he could support pleas for funds made by the Minister of Public Works in cabinet, pleas which would lead to some improvement in the present disastrous and inadequate situation.
This may be one way in which the Minister of the Environment could polish his tarnished image among the fishermen. Having taken away their fishing bounty, their sick mariner's benefits, their swordfishing, salmon fishing and whaling industry, to name but a few, the minister-I can assure him-holds about as much respect among the fishermen as a faulty compass which they know will never lead them in the right direction. Perhaps if the Minister of the Environment spent more time with his colleagues devising policies for our fishermen, rather than attempting to make cheap, partisan politics out of our need for fishing limits on the high seas, as he tried to do at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, our fishermen would have more faith in this government than is now evidenced.
The minister is well aware that our party stated as a matter of policy that we, as a government, would adopt and recognize the principle that Canada and other coastal states own the fishing resources on and over their respective continental shelves and slopes, that the management of these fisheries resources is the responsibility of the coastal state, that other states may only fish such resources with the permission of the coastal state, and in implementing this policy Canada will provide adequate surveillance so that swift action can be taken when Canadian interests are threatened or violated.
That, Mr. Speaker, is our policy. That is our stand. That is our position. That is where we have stood for many years. And what did the minister try to do? He said in his speech that the Conservatives are boldly talking about a 50-mile limit. In effect, Mr. Speaker, Conservative spokesmen were asking this government to support Iceland's stand which is, in my opinion, the same in principle as our own. The only difference is that their continental shelf is approximately 50 miles wide, while ours is 200 miles in some areas and much more than this when one considers the Grand Banks off Newfoundland. The minister fooled no one in New Brunswick. He certainly did not fool any of the fishermen in Atlantic Canada. He fooled no one because there is no record of any action taken by this government to support the principles of continental shelf management as enunciated by Iceland.

speechtext:
That is the point we are trying to establish. When the minister and his parliamentary secretary say this is their position, I would like to know where in this House they have enunciated that position and placed it on the record. It is nowhere to be seen. By not showing any backbone, this minister and this government have made a mockery of their pledges to Canada's fisheries. They have made a mockery of their proposals for the upcoming Law of the Sea Conference scheduled for November in New York, and for Santiago, Chile, in 1974. They have robbed us of support for our proposals from Iceland and other countries, which support will be sorely needed if we are to obtain control of the fishing resources on our continental shelf.

June 7, 1973

Partisan politics will never be a substitute for practical policies. Instead of trying to intentionally mislead the fishermen and the fishing interests of Atlantic Canada, as the Minister of the Environment tried to do at St. Andrews, I suggest that he should try to remember we are still in opposition and that he and his colleagues, as long as they are the government, share the responsibility of proposing a policy that is acceptable to the majority of countries in attendance at the Law of the Sea Conference.
I remind the minister that the problems of the fishing industry are not only the concern of his department: they are also the concern of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp); the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand); the Minister of Public Works; the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson), for surveillance; the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), for unemployment insurance; the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), for marketing; the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), for plant development; and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), for pricing and quality control. These are but a few of the ministers directly involved. Each one of these ministers has a relatively important role to play in the over-all development of our fishing industry.
There is every indication that there will be more government activity in the future; this is something which will have to be worked out between the government and the industry. In my opinion the government has certain responsibilities to this industry, such as the enforcement of regulations, conservation, biological research and the negotiation of international agreements. However, the industry should be permitted to assume certain responsibilities, such as the proper way in which to utilize the resource, the type and size of the ships required to catch the fish, the location of processing plants and the marketing of the catch, as well as the right to research new markets.
There should be one common goal to this over-rail policy; that is, the achievement of an adequate return for our fishermen and processors in relation to the effort made and the capital invested. To bring this about we need to process high quality fish in a form acceptable to the market. For far too long our fishermen have been treated as second-class citizens.
The prime requirement, of course, is some assurance that the fishing resource will always be available. Therefore, in my opinion the results obtained at the upcoming Law of the Sea Conference are vitally important to Atlantic Canada. In this regard I am concerned that the Minister of the Environment may not have the wholehearted support of his cabinet colleagues for his proposal to manage the fisheries on our continental shelf. I cannot help but wonder about the stand that will be taken at this conference by Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs. From the answers given this afternoon by the Minister of the Environment, obviously he has personal views on the course to be followed but he does not have the backing of the government. In my opinion he misled his audience in St. Andrews and he is misleading Canadian fishermen today. Until his stand is backed by the entire cabinet we will not have a clue as to where the govern-
Fisheries
ment will stand when it comes before the Law of the Sea Conference.
The Minister of the Environment speaks about continental shelf management of our fishing resources as though it is something new which he has conceived. What arrogance and what nonsense! I remind him and the House that it was in 1952 that Chile, Ecuador and Peru, in their Santiago declaration, asserted full jurisdiction over the sea to 200 miles from their coasts or to such greater widths as might be necessary to protect in full the rights and well-being of their nationals as the three governments concerned might see fit. Perhaps it is only fitting that the next Law of the Sea Conference will be held in Santiago, because the Santiago declaration did more than any other action or document to launch the nations of the world on a course seeking an acceptable revision of the law of the sea.
In my opinion it is vitally important that the government of Canada, with the support of the opposition, present a united front at the next Law of the Sea Conference so that meaningful progress can be made. We must know who owns the sea bed, who has the right to exploit the minerals of he sea bed and how, where and to what depths this will be done. We must know how far out to sea the living resources of the sea belong to the coastal state. None of this will be easy. I say this, for in the preliminary consultations very few governments have shown any real concern about their sharing or about the whole world's interest in protecting the marine environment. When taking this stand they are only enforcing their present actions on our own continental shelf.
At present we know that some 2,000 fishing vessels are operating in the ICNAF area off the east coast. This increased fishing effort is, in effect, robbing us blind and is contributing to our declining fishery resources. The minister can claim that the countries belonging to ICNAF have agreed to fixed quotas-and I understand the quotas that have been established-but I believe it is our responsibility, as the coastal state, to carry out surveillance of these ships in order to monitor the quotas and also to inspect the fishing equipment to see if it is in accordance with ICNAF regulations.
It is for this reason I suggested to the Minister of the Environment, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), that the minister's department take over the four surplus destroyer escorts of the Canadian armed forces. This is not a new idea. Last year, when announcing control of its waters up to 200 miles from its coast, Mexico negotiated the purchase of ten fleet mineweepers, 215-feet long, from the United States navy. These World War II ships were mothballed at San Diego. They are being used as offshore patrol vessels on both the Gulf and Pacific coasts of Mexico. This type of surveillance off Canada's east coast is long overdue. I hope the minister will take immediate steps to beef up our surveillance capability.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 50 or even 25 years ago when marine resources were or seemed endless and when our fishing fleets were almost at the handicraft level, the motion presented today by the leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) would have been of very little interest and it might not have come to the mind of hon. members to discuss such a matter, at least in the way we are discussing it today. But in recent years, with the advent and development of technology in the fishing industry as in all other industrial sectors, with the appearance of those fishing fleets and floating plants that invade our international and domestic waters, with the advent also of this technology used by our own Canadian fishing fleet, and the very great importance of the fishing industry for the Canadian economy, it has become necessary to change the criteria, since with all the development of this modern technology, we are beginning to fear desperately that our once endless resources be wiped out.
And in recent years it has become evident that the international law was less and less adapted to the new problems and needs deriving from the accelerated development of that technology. That is particularly evident as regards marine environment matters. And when we talk about environment we must not think only in terms of water pollution. The marine environment covers everything concerning the fishing industry.
About 400 years ago, Grotius wrote that most things were getting depleted through excessive use, but that such was not the case with the sea. The sea, he said, could not be depleted either through shipping or through fishing, in other words, through either of both uses that could then be made of it.
The traditional concepts of the law of the sea are unavoidably based on the hypotheses reflected in that assertion from one of the most emminent publicists of the law of the sea. Unfortunately, the nature itself of problems calling for regulations through the law of the sea has been radically changed by modern technology and the development of the law failed to keep pace with the development of technology.
Therefore, Grotius has excuses for not having foreseen the long range implications of technological progress as regards the law of the sea. In his time, since he lived towards the end of the XVIth century and in the beginning of the XVIIth, he could not ask himself for instance, whether nuclear ships and super tankers could be included in the definition of the "innocent passage", whether radioactive waste and nerve gas could be thrown into the sea under the principle of high-sea freedom, whether some protection should be a prerequisite to the drilling off our shores and whether modern fishing fleets more impressive than the Spanish Armada should be free to fish at will in the open sea.
As for us, we would have no excuse for ignoring modern technology's consequences on regulations devised in the
remote ages of sailing boats and old empires. Uses of the sea have been multiplied since Grotius' time. Today, the sea can be depleted through over-fishing, as the one that is unfortunately practised every day, and it is up to us to develop a new law to prevent such a catastrophe.
Canada has a prime interest in all aspects of the law of the sea; this is readily evident when one considers the length of our coast and our dependency on high sea transportation because of our position as an important trading nation. Everybody knows that Canada has taken part in all efforts aimed at establishing new and better adapted rules in line with the new uses of the oceans. Canada's involvement in the 1958 and 1960 conferences is well known, but on many occasions since then we have tried to find solutions to yet unsolved problems, including the limit of territorial waters, as well as the nature and extent of the rights of coastal states over fisheries resources. Even though some progress has been made on those questions at the international level, we have a long way to go before unanimity is achieved. Some states are advocating strictly regional and even domestic solutions; others want a single limit with regard to the maritime sovereignty and other forms of maritime jurisdiction, but this, of course, is a potential source of conflict.
A complete review of all the principles of the 1958 Convention is not desirable and could lead to a return to anarchy and chaos. It remains that the third Conference on the law of the sea scheduled for next fall and the summer of 1974 in Santiago, Chile, will have to study a number of problems that have never been settled satisfactorily. I am thinking more specifically of the review of the rights and duties of the states in the area of conservation and management of maritime living resources, in the light of the growing depletion of those resources as the fishing techniques became more industrial, as I already indicated at the beginning of my remarks. I find it abnormal that some nations should make heavy investments to protect their spawning rivers, as in the case of the Atlantic and Pacific salmon, and that in so doing they should sacrifice the enormous profits they would have made by develop-ping the hydro-electrical energy of those same rivers to find that this very fish which they tried to protect is being caught without any discrimination, by anyone at all, as soon as it starts migrating. Canada believes that the coastal and long distance fishing states should realize that a rationnal system of conservation, management and exploitation of fisheries is necessary in the interest of all. On the one hand, to allow fishing until the last fish is caught would be insanity while, on the other hand, the conflicts and chaos that total prohibition by a coastal state would entail should be avoided.
From Canada's point of view, first of all the international community must provide for special rights and duties of coastal states and set up at the same time new regulations for high sea fishing which will take into account both the need for an equitable distribution of profits and the importance of a rational development of resources.
Mr. Speaker, do I have to refer my colleagues to the stand taken and the suggestion made-which Canada approved-during the environment conference in Stockholm? The material that was published and released to all

The freedom of the seas cannot mean "freedom to exhaust the resources of the sea". Mr. Speaker, I repeat that marine resources are very important, not only for a large number of Canadians but for all our country, and in particular for those I am most concerned about, for most if not all of the constituents of the riding I have the honour to represent. It is a vital industry for these people and 1 suggest that it is the responsibility of both our leaders and those who exploit these resources to do it in a rational manner.
Fisheries are not the only area, Mr. Speaker, in which we have realized, unfortunately a bit too late, that our natural resources are being unconsideredly exploited. The same thing happened to forests in the province of Quebec, for instance, where there used to be numerous and very thick forests. They were exploited unconsideredly so that we find ourselves today in an alarming situation and that is why our governments have dealt with this issue, perhaps a bit late. Of course, I cannot blame the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) and the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) for taking a strong stand on such a crucial problem, and I understand their feelings because they are the feelings of their constituents and the fishermen in the areas they represent.

I realize that everything has not been done and if everything was done at the same time, I wonder what would be the use of having successive parliaments. Fisheries have evolved like any other area and that is why every successive Parliament is faced with problems and must find solutions to the best of its ability in the best interests of the people.
Mr. Speaker, we must therefore take the necessary steps to protect those resources. As I said earlier, I am very concerned with fisheries and on the matter of the depletion of those resources, one cannot remain silent.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, we must protect those resources on which a large number of Canadians depend, including my fellow citizens from Bonaventure-Iles de la Madeleine, while acknowledging that other countries are interested in establishing a functional system offshore under which Canada would have priority rights, a system that will also recognize that others are entitled to a fair share of the benefits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very important motion before us for debate gives us the opportunity of speaking on this subject. The government is being urged by members of the House to implement policies that are in the best interests of this country and our fishermen. The motion deals with fishery resources on and over the continental shelf and slope, as well as adequate surveillance.
First of all, I must mention that before implementing any policy or considering anything that will improve our fishing industry it is important to consider our air and sea rescue operations, particularly in British Columbia. These operations have proven to be rather ineffective at times and have been criticized in respect of poor performance and lack of immediate action. Steps must be taken to bring about improved air-sea rescue operations. I am sure hon. members of this House are agreed that something should be done in this direction in order that Canadian fishermen can operate in an effective and safe manner while harvest-

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
ing one of the most important resources of this country. It is imperative, if we are to expand our fishing operations and if we want safety for our fishermen, that this be treated as a priority matter. Fish stocks have been declining over the years, not because of Canadian fishermen but because we have allowed our territorial waters, just as has happened with the territorial waters of Iceland, to be gradually depleted by foreign fishing fleets.
I welcome, also, the amendment to the motion before us, which I seconded, to the effect that this House assert ownership by Canada of anadromous fish spawned within our borders and the exclusive right to harvest the same. The views expressed in the House today will go a long way toward the formulation of policies that will bring longterm benefits to this country.
The question of the extent of a country's territorial boundaries has arisen many times in many parts of the world. Many countries which depend on fishing and the fishing industry as a major source of revenue and as a matter of national interest are taking action to protect this interest. We have recently witnessed the action taken by Iceland to extend its territorial waters in order to preserve its fishery resources. With the gradual depletion of these resources, Iceland now clings precariously to the edge of an economic precipice, as it finds no alternative to taking such Lilliputian action as is necessary against Great Britain in order to preserve the economic health of its country.
We have also witnessed the action taken by Uruguay, Ecuador, Peru and Chile to extend their territorial waters and fishing rights to 200 miles from shore. We witnessed an earlier declaration by Argentina to extend its fishing rights over the Patagonian shelf. This is the kind of action these countries find necessary to preserve their resources and prevent other countries from depriving them of their livelihood.
Here in Canada we are also faced with the encroachment of foreign fishing vessels within our waters, contributing to the gradual depletion of our fishery resources. It is not sufficient to have a 12-mile limit as this is merely an invitation to other countries to take advantage of our ground-fish resources which extend to the edge of the continental shelf, or of our salmon and herring which are spawned in this country and are the resources of Canada.
There is no doubt that the fishery resources in the waters adjacent to our coastlines must be conserved and developed in the interests of Canadians today and of future generations. The rapid increase in the world fishing effort and efficiency has focused attention on the fact that unless adequate safeguards are taken the marine resources which have played such a vital role in the development of the Canadian economy will be harvested by foreign fishing fleets.
Fishing resources harvested by Canadian fishermen in or out of Canadian territorial waters are also exploited by fishermen of other countries in the high seas adjacent to Canadian territorial waters. Unless positive action is taken by the Government of Canada to enforce the Canadian maritime boundaries and to extend these boundaries beyond the present 12-mile limit, there can be no planned program of fisheries management and conservation. If, however, action can be taken by this country to preserve its interests, then Canadians engaged in the pri-

mary fishing operation and in the many processing industries will be assured of a means of livelihood for many generations to come.
As a member representing a large coastal section of British Columbia it is in my interest and in the interest of fishermen in my constituency to ensure that steps are taken now to safeguard the marine resources which are adjacent to the coastlines of Canada. One of our weaknesses is that we cannot compete economically and on the same scale as the Japanese and/or the Russian fishing fleets. As a result, we must develop and implement a policy that will give us jurisdiction over our fishery resources in the waters adjacent to our coastlines, to the edge of the continental shelf and slope and if necessary to the limit of 200 miles in order that we can conserve and develop these resources.
There is no doubt that the principle of the 200-mile limit must be enforced, not only to 200 miles but also farther than that because the contintental shelf off the east coast of Canada extends in some cases 300 or 400 miles. We must develop a policy by which we can direct our attention toward better conservation to sustain yield operations, toward enforcement of anti-pollution laws and toward measures that will ensure that our fishery resource will continue to be a healthy sector of the Canadian economy.
In conclusion, I insist that this country must enforce its authority in defending the rights of Canadian fishermen to fish unmolested in their own waters. It must also be prepared to enforce its authority up to the edge of the continental shelf and slope, and even up to the limit of 200 miles which is the limit we may have to impose in order to preserve our fishery resources.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to contribute a few minutes to this debate on the welcome motion by the leader of our party. He made clear the policy we stated at the Atlantic conference in September of last year and specifically one of the many recommendations to the effect that we would extend Canada's managerial control to the extremeties of the continental shelf for conservation and management of our marine resources.
It was pleasing, also, to note that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) welcomed the position of our leader. I congratulate him on following the lead of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) who also has the habit of stealing some of our policies. Now all the minister has to do is to get together with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and pound some sense into his head so that the government can move forward to make its clear case at the Law of the Sea Conference.
Since many former speakers have been taking credit for what they did and said over the years even before we Newfoundland members arrived in Ottawa, I am glad to see that the minister is finally coming around to listening to the many pleas we have made to him in the last five years on conservation of our resources and on the provision of meaningful surveillance. It took us five years, Mr. Speaker, and after a few battles I think he is beginning to see the light.
June 7, 1973

However, the leader of our party said, and rightly, that because the Law of the Sea Conference was finally taking place we should not get too confident that the minister will have his policies or objectives accepted immediately. It took a couple of years even to get agreement on an agenda from the other nations. But I am sure everyone in the House who is interested will wish him well. I mention this because our fishing industry is deteriorating even though the minister has such high hopes, which is indicated by the reams of releases which come out of his office. I must say that of all the paper coming out of government offices giving members glad tidings of great things to come, his office must hold the record. I mention this also because we have a problem on our hands right now which must be corrected immediately.
If I might refer to my own province, Mr. Speaker, our patrol capability leaves much to be desired. The foreign draggers must have a great time teasing the Cape Friels, for example, which could not catch a dory at low speed. Even the tracker squadron surveillance operation of the Department of National Defence is meaningless because they fly at predetermined hours and are not available at the time when foreign draggers are fishing within our boundaries. The minister and his department, for some reason or other, in respect of the reports coming in from the district officials take the word of these officials rather than the word of the fishermen.
I had a phone call from a fisherman last year who, while he was talking to me, was watching a foreign dragger tie up at a CNR dock and dump its offal when reports were coming in that all draggers were outside the limits. The department made a token arrest, however, of a Canadian dragger. I wonder what political implications were inherent in this instance. While we are waiting for the extension of our continental shelf, what are the 17,000 fishermen in Newfoundland to do?
This year the ice blockage along much of our coastline delayed the execution of the fisheries for many hundreds of fishermen. When I bring the matter to the attention of the minister he tells me this is not so because his officials have told him it is not so. And while he does not believe the representations of members, and in turn the fishermen, for some reason or other the government has not been able to come up with an unemployment or catch insurance plan to satisfy the industry, under the guise that fishermen are self-employed. I wonder what we are waiting for. Do we wait until the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who is here, comes up with his master plan which will take from three to five years to complete?
The minister also mentioned earlier the direction of his department's effort, and particularly that he is putting another $46 million into a vessel-building program. Fine and dandy, I say, But we have a good vessel-building program now whereby Newfoundland fishermen can get, through federal and provincial programs, 90 per cent of the cost of a longliner; but on the other hand, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) does not have enough money in his budget to provide the necessary wharfage facilities for these longliners. This emphasizes the lack of, and need for a comprehensive Canadian fisheries policy, which is now a patchwork system of various departments, both
Fisheries
federal and provincial, going off in different directions and wasting millions of dollars.
The fishermen of Newfoundland are a completely frustrated lot of citizens, wondering what kind of legislators we are in Ottawa. Newfoundland joined confederation in 1949 because of the great benefits of our nation. True, there have been many benefits and I am glad this has come about, as are most Newfoundland citizens. But the Fathers who made the deal up here in Ottawa did not realize that the federal government would brush aside our little fishing industry as a little speck in their national goals. They did not realize, and evidently did not convey the idea that fishing was our basic resource and that it dictated our unique way of life. Those who governed after 1949 caught the industrialization disease, a disease which even today we cannot get rid of in our greed and our search for oil and other minerals. Unfortunately, we in our proud province still do not realize the environmental value and peacefulness of our lifestyle, a quality of life that is fast disappearing in our greed for wealth regardless of the cost.
The fishing industry in Newfoundland is our basic resource and we must protect this industry at all costs. We must protect the small fishing communities and the fishermen citizens who are as good Canadians as those whom we push to the big cities, citizens who because of fisheries policies have tried to relocate to growth centres to their detriment and disturbance. The fishery in Newfoundland is analogous to that of Iceland because we are fighting for survival. Iceland, as an independent nation, is dependent for 80 per cent of its economy on the fisheries. Can anyone blame it for the action it took to reinforce its survival?
The Minister of the Environment keeps repeating that we do not, and should not have to resort to gunboat diplomacy to protect our livelihood. I ask him: What do we do. Do we wait for the countless studies and programs he has announced? Do we wait for support facilities, the responsibility for which will be handed over by the Department of Public Works to the Department of Fisheries? Do we wait for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to sign the transfer of responsibilities so that the minister can get on with the job of providing small craft harbours to our fishermen? Do we wait for the minister to believe the members of the opposition from Newfoundland who are on his side but he does not know it? Do we wait for him and his government to show some backbone and tell the foreign nations that we were not aware of the value of the fishery resources and did not provide the factory ships and the trawlers necessary to compete for this lucrative resource?
Is it any wonder that the fishermen of Newfoundland have lost their hope of regaining their livelihood in the fishing industry? Is it any wonder that my colleague the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) had to make an issue of the political speech the minister made in New Brunswick a short time ago? Is it any wonder that I as a Member of Parliament, in my frustration when foreign draggers were raping the shores of my district two years ago, reluctantly threatened to take up arms together with my fishermen to keep these foreign draggers from ravaging our shores and denying our citizens their rights?

Fisheries
No one in Canada wants to resort to gunboat diplomacy. The minister is either being partisan or is still not aware of what poverty is. He is not aware of what frustration is and what the consequences might be of denying Canadians their rights: if he had been, he would not have made the statements he did.
Since time does not permit me to go on much longer, let me conclude by saying to the minister that all he has to do is trust Canadians regardless of their political leanings. Let him bring his case to the Law of the Sea Conference with our support. Let him bring Bill C-4 before the House of Commons so as to provide the support facilities necessary for the fishermen of the Atlantic region. Let him bring in his new programs for the provision of vessels to allow Canadian fishermen to take advantage of our resources. He should get on with the job of supplying the new patrol vessel which he announced. But let him remember the pledge of this government to guarantee equality of opportunity to all Canadians wherever they may live, which should include the fishermen of the Atlantic region and will benefit all Canadians.
