subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I have decided to take part in the debate on the motion presented by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), you will permit me to say that the government took action quite a long time before the idea of protecting the fisheries resources on our continental shelves and slopes ever crossed the mind of the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party.
The opposition days in the House, designated to deal with ways and means resolutions, do not offer the Canadian people anything new. We have already studied in its minute details the subject presently before the House in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, as well as in that on Fisheries and Forestries. Because what we heard today had already been said on many occasions by ministers and department officials, I say this is stale news.
The opposition is really limited in the choice of measures it wishes to suggest to the government. How lucky the Canadian people are, Mr. Speaker, to have had, since 1963, a government which is so concerned with their welfare and which presents legislative measures, not only for this generation but also for future ones. I would like to quote only the legislation passed by this Parliament on our territorial limit of 12 miles, and I remind this House that we have shown the way to a number of other countries by passing a legislation to protect our environment as far as 100 miles off our coasts, north of the 60,h parallel.
With regard to the limits beyond territorial waters, several proposals have been made by various countries during the international conferences that have taken place, in order that the state may exercise its jurisdiction over the off-shore resources as far as 200 miles.
In addition to the jurisdiction over the off-shore resources, some states also want to broaden their jurisdiction over fisheries, and others would be prepared to take into account fishing done on the high seas for generations. There are some treaties to be considered and Canada, through its Secretary of State for External Affairs and its

Department of Fisheries has signed protocols with several countries concerning provisions to control fisheries within the 12-mile territorial limits. The negotiations were not easy, and we are grateful to those two ministers for the achievements. There is another type of jurisdiction with which we are concerned and that is pollution control. The Canadian government has already indicated that it advocates very strict regulations. On the other hand-that is well-known-our neighbours to the south, the United States, hardly accept the policy of the Canadian government in the area of pollution control on our coasts.
The Canadian position is known to everybody, since it has been outlined a number of times at the UNFAO, to the effect that we want to be the owners of the fishing resources on our continental shelves and slopes. We even went further in defining a continental shelf, since we have always maintained the position that the Canadian continental shelf extends to the continental limit, that is the shelf itself plus the slope or part of it.
In fishing matters, the government has defined two kinds of jurisdiction: that which the coastal state can exercise on fishing resources, as there is no longer a question of sticking to the previous system of non-interference, according to which anyone can fish at will. The coastal state must preserve the right to manage resources, including the right to set quotas. The government proposals still go further; it is asking that the coastal state be the sole beneficiary of certain marine species.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) has already pointed out that some anadromous species such as the Atlantic salmon should not be fished in open sea, lest it become depleted. We are endeavouring on the Atlantic coast to preserve the salmon-especially the Gaspe salmon-and the countries practising that fishing should be more conscious of the conditions. This is why, Mr. Speaker, we must continue to prod the northern countries into preserving that species and we know that the Minister of Environment has performed significant work to that effect.
The motion of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) reads as follows and I quote:
. . . the management of these fisheries resources are the responsibility of the coastal state, that other states may only fish such resources with the permission of the coastal state;
As for the Gulf of St. Lawrence, we are facing a very special problem: the presence of the Islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, which belong to France.
During an external affairs and national defence committee debate, Mr. Alan Beesley, legal adviser and general manager of the Bureau of legal services, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), concerning the islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, had this to say about the negotiations, and I quote:
They are in abeyance at the moment... Our problem is that we have had a series of negotiations and over the course of years, literally, that these negotiations have taken, the position has developed to the point where we could be on the verge of an agreement. The problem is, in simple terms, that the French government originally took the position that St. Pierre and Miquelon were entitled to a shelf such as any other piece of land and therefore the equidistance principle must apply in determining the boundary line between their continental shelf and ours.

We took the position that the convention on the continental shelf to which both countries are party clearly envisages special circumstances, refers to the problem as special circumstances in which the equidistance principle would not be deemed to apply, and they said this is a classic case for the application of the special circumstances rule. So that meant we then had to get into negotiations to bring the two positions together.
The tentative outline of an agreement which has been worked out and which both governments must consider is rather complex because it is not based on a simple territorial acquisition. It is based on an attempt to determine what the real needs of the respective parties are, what the real interests are and where the point of accommodation lies. In other words, it is not simply a case of drawing a line on a map and saying there is the edge of the continental shelf.
It is conceivable, for example, that France might accept a lesser continental shelf if it could obtain certain types of benefits which we would normally not be willing to grant. So this is about all I really can say at the moment because the negotiations are confidential.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the government ensures an appropriate control so that swift steps may be taken to safeguard the interests of Canadians, especially those of fishermen on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts.
The association which exists in France concerning the islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon in the Gulf of St. Lawrence is an excellent example of the complexity of negotiations at the international level. Hon. members of the opposition blame the government for not taking immediate action concerning the fishing rights on the continental shelf of Canada.
What a calamity for Canada if diplomatic negotiations were the responsibility of the hon. leader of the opposition. How would he succeed in having Canada's positions accepted at the international conferences since he cannot even sell his own ideas on national policy to members of his own caucus.
With regard to negotiations on the international level, it is not an easy task and the government must take the lead in the conservation of our territorial waters and fisheries resources on and over the continental shelves and slopes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF OWNERSHIP AND ACTION TO PROTECT FISHERIES RESOURCES OVER THE CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise this evening to support the motion of the hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). When one thinks of the power at the negotiating table mentioned by my hon. friends across the way, one wonders what power the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) may have when he arrives at an international conference without even the blessing of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) for the proposal that he plans to present. Not only can he not get the consent of all his confreres to put forward this proposal, but he cannot get the consent of the minister who is particularly charged with that responsibility.
At this stage of a debate, Mr. Speaker, pretty well all that can be said has been said. I might take a moment, however, to review what I consider to be that situation as
Fisheries
far as the Canadian fishery is concerned, or at least to speak of that with which I am familiar, the Atlantic fishery. The fishermen on the Atlantic coast are filled with uncertainty. We have seiners encroaching upon the territory of the weirs, big vessels encroaching upon the territory of little ones, foreigners encroaching upon the territory of Canadian vessels, lobstermen facing the depletion of lobster grounds by the encroachment of foreign vessels, lobstermen faced with broken promises by this government with regard to research which was to take place on the effect of fishing of offshore lobsters on inshore grounds. We have the effective loss of the whaling industry, the swordfishing industry, the salmon industry and the sealing industry. There is a good deal of uncertainty in the industry about the future of scallops and herring because of recent measures taken by the department.
New standards for fishing vessels have been brought in without any meaningful consultation with the men who operate them. The regulations involve not only those aspects of vessel construction and management which concern the quality of fishing but also changes which recently came into effect in regard to steamship regulations and the measurement of vessels. The regulations now require extremely small vessels to undergo the same type of rigorous inspection as steamships. Last, but not least, is the uncertainty of our fishermen about whether they are going to have a harbour big enough to hold their vessels once they acquire the new vessels that will be needed to comply with the requirements.
As we have learned in committee, in Atlantic Canada wharves are in a deplorable state of disrepair and require many millions of dollars to bring them up to standard. The future of the small fish plant operators in my riding is very uncertain. There are inconsistent inspection procedures, and apparently ad hoc standards. A fish plant and the product may pass inspection one day but not the next. There is an absence of meaningful help or guidance from the Department of the Environment as far as fisheries are concerned, and there is apparent callousness on the part of those charged with this responsibility toward small fish plant owners.
The vocabulary of this administration includes such words as "regulation", "protection", "inspection", "service" and "rationalization". Very seldom do we hear officials of the Department of the Environment or the minister speak of the promotion of the fisheries, encouragement of the fisheries, assistance to the fisheries or diversification of fish plants and fishing operations. This resolution, Mr. Speaker, can go some distance toward securing dependability of supply for our fishermen and fish plants. Within this context, however, there must be harbour facilities for big vessels, small vessels and intermediate vessels. Also, we must provide assistance to fish plants: there clearly is a need for large, small and intermediate operators.
Mr. Speaker, I heartily endorse the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). The amendment falls into line very well with the context and import of the motion of the leader of our party. I was encouraged, too, by the minister's statement about the changing attitude of various countries toward the imposi-

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
tion of control of our continental shelf to a 200-mile limit. I was concerned, however, by the answer he gave this afternoon to questions which indicated that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not been won over to that view.
The ICNAF agreement on quotas represents a forward step in protecting and controlling our fishery resources off our coasts. Whether the Canadian fishermen will benefit in fact has yet to be decided. So far the result has been that fewer herring and haddock have been landed than would have been landed if the ICNAF agreement had not been reached. Contrary to the minister's statement this afternoon, not enough herring were provided for in the quota to keep our fishing fleet or our fish plants operating. In the Bay of Fundy there is a seiner fleet potentially able to catch some 200,000 tons of herring on our traditional grounds but now, under the ICNAF agreement, they are limited to 5,000 tons which is barely enough to supply one vessel with an adequate annual catch. Also, the over-all catch, as several hon. members have mentioned, has been declining annually. Our fishermen believe that this is the result of the rape of our resources by the vessels of foreign fleets operating off our coasts.
Despite the minister's assurances to the contrary, we have no way of knowing how much fish is actually being caught by many of these foreign vessels. There are 2,000 such vessels operating off our coasts. Until there are practical controls or controls which are negotiated with respect to the size of catches, the means of catching or the technique of catching the ICNAF agreement will be suspect so far as our fishermen are concerned.
What of the 200-mile limit? Here I am talking of Canada's surveillance capability. There is little use proposing a 200-mile limit or a continental shelf limit unless Canada has the capability to patrol this area at sea to make sure that our sovereignty is not abused. At the moment, on the east coast we have one vessel capable of providing surveillance and enforcement. We have heard proposals respecting another vessel which will come into being some years hence. I am astounded at the press release issued by the minister on May 11 which said in so many words that Canada has increased its aerial surveillance to the point where we will now have one flight per week of a tracker aircraft.

speechtext:
True, it is about 60 seconds. Tied in with that we must consider our rescue capability. To me, a maritime Canadian who has confidence in the ability of our seamen, who is proud of our maritime heritage and knows the capability of our seamen to cope in the worst weather conditions as well as in the best weather, it is particular galling to find that almost always when one of our vessels gets into trouble, or one of our fishermen needs to be rescued, the rescuer is either one of our own fishing vessels or the United States Coastguard.
The situation will be totally ridiculous if one considers it in the light of a 200-mile territorial sea limit. Certainly, if we are to have a 200-mile territorial sea we must have the ability to do the necessary lifesaving and patrolling that will be needed. A worth-while suggestion in this regard was made by one of my colleagues last week. He suggested that serious consideration should be given to taking over the four destroyer escorts which have been mothballed in Halifax. These destroyers are admirably suited to this task. They are fast and seaworthy and can carry a helicopter, which could be of vital use in the event of a disaster at sea not only in rescuing people but in flying them back to the coast where they can receive medical attention.
Much has been said about the 12-mile limit and the fact that the Liberal government of the 1960s was responsible for declaring it. Taken as a bald fact, that may be so. However, such statements ignore that the concept was advanced by the Conservative government at the Law of the Sea Conference in 1958, and that the idea very nearly won international acceptance. That was the ground-breaking episode with regard to that matter. The Liberal government of the sixties was merely following suit, merely following the line that had already been established by the former Conservative government.
What has been the effect of that unilateral declaration of the 12-mile limit? In many instances the declaration has not had any effect because every nation wants to protect its own interests. But is has affected our lobstermen who are unable to fish on their traditional grounds while American boats fish there, because presumably those American boats have some traditional right to fish in Canadian waters. I do not know whether a solution could be found, but if one is not found shortly there will be another shooting war because the Nova Scotia lobster fishermen, faced with declining catches and knowing the effect of the offshore lobster catches, are in no mood to sit idly by. They do not appreciate trying to catch haddock, halibut or hake while American fishermen are inside our 12-mile limit catching lobster which they may not be able to take.
I want to say in closing that I am proud of my country and proud of its maritime heritage. We cannot, as Canadians, stand by and see our maritime resources depleted by others who come to our shores. We can share. We have enough resources that we can share with other countries, under proper management, a portion of them. But we, the members of this House, must protect our citizens as well as the various species of fish. Whales, scallops and lobsters may need protection; but so our fishermen. Independent

June 7, 1973

fishermen and independent fish plant owners are in danger of extinction as well. I believe that is something this House and this government ought to be concerned about. We must declare our title to the continental shelf and/or the 200-mile limit. We must agree to persuade others to recognize our ownership and right of control. We must have the capability, as well, to control that area. The resources of the sea are ours, but we must act soon to ensure our continued right to lay claim to them.

As a result of this resolution I was named as a special raporteur to report back to the assembly on this question. In preparing my report to the assembly I called upon the expertise which is available within our government. speechtext:
I would like to know that position. The Canadian people have a right to know whether any party in this House is about to sell out the Canadian patrimony which I feel exists in these resources. As far as I am concerned, these resources, whether in the north or off our coasts, are the heritage of the Canadian people from coast to coast, regardless of the province in which they live. That position has not been clearly stated in this House by anyone. I hope the various political parties will begin to at least take some clear position in this regard.
It was the official policy of the Conservative party in the last election to make the Yukon a province within five years of taking office. This was in Conservative campaign material. I feel strongly that for the Yukon, which has a population of 20,000, to turn over the immense resources of that territory-everyone familiar with the Yukon realizes that the economy is controlled by perhaps 15 to 30 individuals-would be tantamount to creating a Canadian Kuwait in our north.
We ought to consider seriously in relation to our northern resources a system different from that which was adopted when the provinces were first created. The situation has changed dramatically. We now realize that resources are limited. They are a much more important element in our economy; they have a greater potential for the country's future well-being than any other factor. Surely all parties in the House should be giving this subject much more reasoned attention than has been the case up to now.
There is one way in which we could do something about these resources. Unfortunately it is a matter which has been neglected by this government. I refer to the apparent helplessness of the Canada Development Corporation to act in areas where attention is badly needed now. If we had a resource development corporation which could invest heavily in oil and mineral resource development and exploration in the Northwest Territories, in the Yukon and offshore the whole question whether Canadian or provincial jurisdiction applies would become less important. We would see, in effect, a strong resource development corporation controlling a key portion of these resources in the name and on behalf of the people of Canada.
This would be a solution, but apparently the government is not yet ready to create a development corporation which could do these things. The corporation which presently exists is designed to assist manufacturing industries in southern Canada. It is designed to provide a safe return to shareholders and to pay out dividends. It cannot contemplate the kind of risk which a natural resource devel-

opment corporation would have to undertake if it were to explore, develop and bring mines and oilfields into production in the north or offshore. For this I have no one to criticize but my own side of the House.
In my view we must move toward control, if not by agreement with the provinces then at least through a resource development corporation to ensure an interest for the Canadian people as a whole in the offshore mineral and oil resources as well as of our mineral and oil resources in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. With the greatest respect to our national press, very few people, especially those in central Canada today, are able to understand the complexities of the issue. Consequently, people like the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) can present any kind of argument and if they are smooth enough and subtle enough they can convince the country that they are sincere and honest. It takes somebody who has a maritime background to be able to recognize that what the minister said today represented a serious withdrawal; the minister was retreating from Moscow. He got involved in the issue of our resources, both inshore and on the continental shelf, and the subject of decisions in international law back in 1958 and later.
These are Canadian resources. They belong to Canada. The difference is that the hon. member has stated in less sophisticated fashion, in less calculating fashion, the position of his government. Therefore we now know that if the present government has a long tenure of office in this country we in Atlantic Canada have had it so far as concerns using our continental shelf resources to our advantage. As a matter of fact, with respect to what he put on the record today I suggest that every member from Atlantic Canada should see it is repeated and sent to all our constituents to allow them to understand the condescending, narrow-minded approach that he and his government have toward our continental resources. speechtext:
We did not mention 200 miles. We mentioned the continental shelf and the continental slopes, which are in the same context. Two hundred miles happens to be the sexy, "in" language in international affairs today, but we mentioned the continental shelf and the continental slope even though we haven't the scientists to back up the position we have taken, scientists that are available to the government.
We moved a second resolution to have the House of Commons express support for the Canadian delegation to the ICNAF conference that began in Copenhagen on Sunday. The Leader of the Opposition is expressing pessimism about imposing quotas, but he did not express any regret that we continue to support ICNAF save with the qualification that Canada may have to determine its own jurisdiction and take its own initiative.
The Minister of the Environment was quite willing to accept our resolution. I can tell Your Honour now that I had discussions with several members of the Canadian delegation, which is led by the former deputy minister of fisheries, who told me they would feel better at ICNAF if they had the expressed support of the House of Commons, the highest court in the land, behind them. But that resolution was rejected. I rose the next day in the House and asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if he would be prepared to bring a resolution before the House expressing support for Canada's position at the ICNAF conference, and that request was rejected. If we can achieve the position-and it is an important principle- that Canada is able to catch whatever fish it can under our quota, it is a step in the right direction. We are not pessimistic there. However, we are pessimistic about enforcing some of the quotas established, with the kind of surveillance which Canada up until now has shown on the east coast.
It is very restrictive for a member to have only 15 minutes in which to present a position on this issue. The minister had 40 minutes in which to speak, and I have only 15 minutes to present my argument. I cannot do it in that time but I do want to leave one more impression with the House. It is that what happens in ICNAF, at the Law of the Sea Conference or in the provision of marine facilities is in one way or another irrelevant to the main issue in this debate. The main issue at stake in this debate and the reason why this resolution is before the House is to challenge the attitude of the federal government toward the fisheries of the nation. This is the most important problem we have. It has nothing to do with the continental shelf or 200 miles. The main issue is the attitude that is developing in this part of Canada toward our marine resources. This is something we would like to change.
Coming in the aftermath of the proceedings on yesterday's resolution when there was a lot of debate about national unity, I would like to make this one last plea, Mr. Speaker. If I could be a bit small, a bit parochial in my comments I would like to mention something originally put forward by my colleague from the west coast of Newfoundland. We are a province, as my colleague mentioned, of 500,000 people. Iceland is a country, a nation of 220,000 people.
When we became part of Canada 24 years ago we gave up our right of self-determination in the fishing industry

because we wanted to become part of Canada and to enjoy the thousands of benefits that flow from being part of such a beautiful country. As I say, we gave up that right in the expectation that Canada would take up the cudgels and protect our rights as part of the Canadian nation.
Now, in Canadian terms fisheries are relatively unimportant. We can accept the statement of my colleague from St. John's West (Mr. Carter) that the fisheries represent only 2 per cent of the gross national product, or the statement by an economist who said the fisheries were the seventh largest industrial endeavour in the hierarchy of the Canadian industrial structure. But the fact remains that in New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island the fisheries represent the most important economic endeavour in our nation. Consequently, it is vital that Canada stand up for our people, that it take an aggressive position, that it show some leadership.
However, we are very afraid that this matter has been pulled down to a political issue within the last few years. We in the Atlantic area are relatively unimportant politically. It will not make very much difference to the national scene whether the Liberal party wins two seats, three seats or five seats in our region in the next election. Consequently, to the party in power today, and possibly to any future government, we may seem to be a very unimportant piece of political real estate. This is what has had a greater impact than any other force on what has happened to our fisheries.
We ask the Canadian government to amend its attitude by even a few degrees on the compass and look at this issue, not as just a cheap, little political move, not in terms of economic importance to Canada but in terms of the livelihood and well-being of the people on the east coast. We want a change in the attitude of the Canadian public and a change in the attitude of this government in terms of the fishing industry on the east and west coasts of Canada. This is our plea. We are not asking for separatism, we are not talking about breaking our ties with Canada- but unless we can get the Canadian nation to change its course substantially and recognize that because we have lost our self-determination to make our own decisions in respect of trade, commerce and all the other aspects of international relationships and agreements, then we have to be a little bit unhappy to be associated with a government that will not stand and be recognized as protecting our rights.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like others I feel it is very difficult to put forward all my ideas in respect of this matter in 15 minutes. For that reason I will try to shorten my remarks and the expression of my thoughts on this motion and the amendment. Let me say that I am extremely proud and honoured to belong to a political party which has had a consistent view about this question for as long as I have been a member. The party which preceded the NDP, namely the CCF, was persistent and constant in its concern about fisheries and the 12-mile international limit. It was consistent in its concern about the international question concerning the continental shelf.
We appreciate the opportunity of speaking on this motion put forward by the Conservative Party. We regret that the motion is deficient in that it does not refer to the salmon fisheries off the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, although we are happy to note that this has been corrected by the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). There is not another ana-dromous fish involved in this, but that is not at the moment a matter of commercial fishing importance. Anyone who has dealt with this subject matter over the years knows it has been an uphill fight. We also know that the motion put forward by the Conservative party is another move in that fight. I must state that the most difficult time we have had in respect of this whole matter was when the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) was minister of fisheries. We met during those years absolute obstinacy coupled with indifference and lack of concern.
I think we should pay our respects to a very tiny nation in this world for its approach to the matter of preserving its fisheries. We should express our appreciation for the tenacity and the foresight of Iceland in this regard. Coastal nations of the world owe a debt to Iceland which they will never be able to repay because it is an emotional debt and a debt with future consequences. It was Iceland that set the precedent for coastal nations in respect of a 12-mile limit. It declared unilaterally a 12-mile limit, and it had to contend with Great Britain in this respect. There was not another nation in the councils of the world that support that position. For all the brave words of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) in recent days and weeks, it is a matter of national regret, on my part at least, that Canada has not declared openly and publicly support for the position of Iceland in its desire to preserve the fisheries of that coastal nation.
Iceland is now talking about a 50-mile limit because that circumscribes an area around Iceland and is an easy way to measure the continental shelf and slope. That 50-mile circumscription pretty well coincides with the continental shelf and slope in relation to Canada. I wish every success to Iceland in its contest with Great Britain.
Precedents in international law have traditionally and historically come about by unilateral action on the part of a state. Very rarely has international law been established by agreement between nations. Britain, or whatever it was called in the early days, unilaterally established a three-mile limit because that was the distance they could cover with their coastal guns. Britain was able to exercise that territorial jurisdiction by saying it could fire three miles
Fisheries
offshore and if foreign fishing vessels came within that distance they were in jeopardy.
It was Iceland that established the 12-mile limit, and this was accepted in the world. Some years ago Peru established a 200-mile fishing zone limit, but that limit had other complications than are conceived in respect of our territorial seas fishing zones. After Canada had consulted with the United States it unilaterally declared a nine-mile fishing zone. This was only after failure at two international conferences on the Law of the Sea and a discussion about putting this subject on the agenda at the United Nations.
Canada's position has been historically weak in the area of establishing authority over our own resources, especially those of the sea. Generally speaking, with one exception, and that was only after approaching the late President Kennedy and guaranteeing that United States, fishermen would have the right to fish within that nine-mile fishing zone and after we had committed ourselves not to infringe upon the so-called historical position of the United States, we have not taken a unilateral position. Apart from that we have sought consensus, agreement and accommodation from other countries to do those things which we ourselves should do for our own preservation and self-respect. Even in respect of the negotiations that took place a short while ago on the U.S.-Canada, or Cana-da-U.S. agreement, namely, the reciprocal fishing agreement, we knuckled under. We refused to stand up and be firm in our position. Unfortunately, that has been the attitude of Canada for too long in matters such as this. What we need is a determination, a strong unilateral declaration, not in fancy words or statements written by speechwriters for the Minister of Fisheries, but actions and declarations which mean something.
Mr. Speaker, if the government wishes any guidance or any advice in respect of how to approach this matter, it need go no further than look to the father-in-law of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), Jimmy Sinclair, becau.se when he was minister of fisheries of this country we knew where we were going in respect of fishery matters. Ever since he left that post and was defeated, Canada's position on fishery matters on the international scene has gone downhill. Had it not been for people like Jimmy Sinclair and George Clark, the deputy minister of fisheries, and their determination we would not have had the Fraser River agreement with the United States, because that agreement was the result of our standing up to the United States and telling it what our position was.
I contrast the position at that time with the weak, lily-livered position taken by the government in respect of the current negotiations which apparently have just concluded with the United States. We do not need fancy speeches by the minister about 200 miles or any other number of miles. Rather, we need a declaration of intent. We need to take action as a nation in so far as our own fisheries are concerned. We must do so for our own integrity and for the sake of our respect and unity.
We have an obligation to future generations in this matter insofar as the food resources of the world are concerned. Up until now, very regrettably, we have treat-

June 7, 1973
Fisheries
ed this obligation as a bargaining item to be dealt with and dealt away in the niceties of our diplomatic relationships with other countries. What that approach has meant for us is that we have been made suckers by other nations of the world. We need a declaration to unify us, a unilateral declaration so that other people will know what we intend to do. In that regard let me read the motion and then ask the House a question. The motion asks that this House accept a certain principle; then it enumerates what it is.
In addition, there is an amendment by my colleague the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in respect of an assertion of ownership by Canada of anadromous fish. The motion states, however, that to implement this policy we must provide adequate surveillance, and so on. All the motion is asking for is a declaration of principle by the House of Commons concerning what our intentions and ideals are. Regardless of the position in respect of the Standing Orders, I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the motion were put by you now it would receive unanimous consent. I do not think anyone in this House disagrees with what it says. I would ask, through you, Mr. Speaker, that the proposition be put to the House that by unanimous consent we call a vote on the amendment and on the motion so that all parties can declare themselves with one voice for Canada.

TRANSPORT-SUBSIDY TO FOREIGN REGISTERED VESSEL, MV "TRAVETAL"-SUGGESTED REQUIREMENT OF CANADIAN REGISTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that we have some order in the House may I direct my remarks to a subject that has aroused many people in eastern Canada. The matter of the Canadian coastal shipping trade has already been raised in the House and in various parts of the country, so much so that many people feel it is no longer a newsworthy issue. It may no longer be a newsworthy issue to some people but it continues to be a contentious issue among political and shipping circles.
When the government of Canada is willing to finance the operation of foreign registered and foreign manned vessels so that they may participate in carrying out Canadian trade between Canadian ports, it is time for us to question seriously the government regarding the overgenerous subsidies that are given to such ships. We find here in Canada a situation in which Canadian ships are being replaced by ships under foreign registry and in which Canadian crews are being replaced by foreign crews.
I can understand the government's argument against the implementation of the Darling report and the government's contention that the operation of foreign manned vessels is much less expensive, but I do not understand it when a Singapore registered vessel such as the MV Trav-etal is guaranteed new subsidies to operate between Canadian ports. Such a situation does not support the government's arguments in this respect.
The vessel Travetal has recently been picketed in Halifax. The operation of this ship owned by Trident Steamships Limited has cost Canadian taxpayers $368,100 in the fiscal year 1972-73 alone. I am not questioning the jurisdictional right of the SIU to picket this particular ship; what I am questioning are the political and legal manoeuvres whereby such ships are allowed to operate at the expense of Canadian taxpayers, and Canadian seamen because they are out of work are forced to sail on ships which do not come under the control of Canadian steamship inspection and marine safety regulations. This is why the SIU or any other seamen's union has the moral right to picket such ships. This is one of the few means whereby our attention can be focused on this issue.
My opinion is that the use of cheap foreign labour and flags of convenience, not only in the coastal trade but also in the future development of offshore and Arctic areas, cannot be tolerated. The oil companies, the shipping interests and the assorted trading companies that control the economics and political life of the Atlantic provinces must be denied the generous concessions that have served their own interests in the past and that cannot contribute to the future prosperity of the area.
In conclusion, I ask the minister-unfortunately he is not here tonight-whether he can justify his actions in permitting the permanent entry into the coastal trade of Canada of the motor vessel Travetal and similar vessels, in terms of the provisions of the Alien Labour Act. I would also ask him to consider the views that I have expressed and to tell the House how and when he hopes to implement the recommendations of the Darling report.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-SUBSIDY TO FOREIGN REGISTERED VESSEL, MV "TRAVETAL"-SUGGESTED REQUIREMENT OF CANADIAN REGISTRY
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would not agree with all the phraseology and the various things said by the previous speaker. If one were to agree with it, it would certainly put things out of kilter. The vessel is a Singapore registered ship, with German officers and a Spanish crew. The owner's address is London, England. In other words, it is owned by the British and the vessel is time-chartered to Trident Steamships Limited of Halifax, Nova Scotia. She carries out a completely roll-on, roll-off general cargo service, the principal cargo being automobiles, between Halifax, Nova Scotia and St. John's, N ewf oundland.
While she is permitted, on account of being a British ship, to engage in the coasting trade of Canada, she is also subject to other sections of the Canada Shipping Act. The one causing the problems relates to the certificates of competency of the master and officers which under the act must be Canadian, as the hon. member said, or others accepted by the minister such as certain Commonwealth certificates. The present officers hold German certificates.
Under the authority given to him by the Canada Shipping Act, the minister on March 6, 1973, exempted the Travetal from the requirements of carrying officers holding Canadian certificates for a period of three months only until June 5, 1973, on condition that the party responsible for the operation submit proposals for compliance with the act. To date no such proposal has been received. The exemption expired on June 5 and has not been renewed. I should like to emphasize that, Mr. Speaker. The purpose of the exemption was to avoid disruption of the service currently provided between Halifax and St. John's, and representations urging this course were received from the Premier of Nova Scotia and representatives of the local International Longshoremen's Union.
Opposition to the exemption comes from the seamen's unions which are strong advocates of the recommendation that the coasting trade of Canada should be reserved for Canadian flag ships. With the expiry of the exemption, the Seafarers International Union took legal action to prevent its renewal. A telegram has been received from the Halifax local of the International Longshoremen's Union urging that the service be allowed to continue. Premier Regan of Nova Scotia has expressed the same concern.
Today, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) sent a telegram to Trident Steamships, to the International Longshoremen's Union and to Premier Regan of Nova Scotia stating that the exemption from the Canada Shipping Act provisions cannot be renewed indefinitely and that adequate time has already been allowed for compliance with the act. Late this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the minister received a new proposal from the operators which is now being taken under advisement.

POST OFFICE-ALLEGED DELAY IN DELIVERY OF FIRST-CLASS MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I asked questions in the House previously concerning unsatisfactory postal service, the Postmaster General (Mr. 
Ouellet) said that he required specifics. I will now list a few definite examples of slow delivery. First, I cite the instance of a letter posted on March 30, 1973, in Red Deer, Alberta, destined for Vancouver. It was delivered to a Vancouver law firm on April 6, seven days later. Second, may I mention delivery of letters between Red Deer and Edmonton, and Red Deer and Calgary, a distance in each case of 100 miles, taking two days. Previously these were delivered the next day.
Third, Rosedale Presbyterian church, Toronto, complained directly to the Postmaster General that a letter posted at noon on Thursday April 26 in Toronto, for delivery in Toronto, was not delivered until the following Monday morning. Fourth, a letter addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) which was posted in Red Deer on May 11 was not received in his office in Ottawa until May 18.
My constituents and others have expressed dissatisfaction also with the handling of mail which has resulted in breakages and other damage to well wrapped and securely tied parcels sent by first-class mail. The question arises whether or not there is any advantage in time and handling when one pays the highest postal rate. Parcels sent out first-class do not seem to arrive any earlier than parcels sent by ordinary parcel post rate, nor are they delivered in any better condition.
It is all very well for the Postmaster General to continue to acclaim the modernization of postal administration with computers and postal codes. Taxpayers are well aware of these changes, if for no other reason than that they pay for them and have had to spend additional hours in adding codes to their mailings both business and personal. When a person receives mail later than within a reasonable delivery period, and in the case of parcels in damaged or broken condition, that person is not interested in hearing again a glorified and detailed description of modern innovations to sort mail, or about the postal code system. On the one hand, the sorting of mail does not mean anything to the recipient or sender if mail is not delivered accurately and on time; on the other hand he is well aware that the computerized equipment is costing taxpayers millions of dollars. He wants to know why mail service has deteriorated to the extent it has over the last two years or so, when can he expect prompt and efficient mail delivery, will parcels be handled with care, as they once were, will letters be delivered to the address on the envelope and not to a residence three or four doors away or to one on the next street, and how long does it take inexperienced employees to become efficient, to read the address and deliver the mail? I do not think these questions are unreasonable or can be passed off with a shrug.
People pay for postal service. They are entitled to efficient and prompt delivery and they are still hoping they will receive the type of service for which they have paid and are paying. Just today I received a letter from a constituent. It is dated June 2, 1973. I should like to read it into the record. It reads:
Dear Mr. Towers:
Someone told me that you had complained about slow-moving mail but needed more proof. I enclose a envelope of the letter I sent to Mr. Reg Johnson whose address is Red Deer, but lives east of Penhold. You might know the person since he is not too far from your place. I sent them a cheque for seed oats on May 4th,
June 7, 1973	COMMONS DEBATES	4565
and they were wondering why I did not pay. I was there later on to get some more seed and stopped payment on the cheque since I figured that the wrong person got hold of it, but they got it all right, 26 days after mailing, so maybe this will prove that somebody is not on his or her toes.
People who are using our mail system expect service. If they do not get good service, they will stop using it. If they stop using it, the cost must rise. The easiest way to have cheaper mail service is to give better service. These points are being brought to the attention of the Postmaster General on behalf of the people whom I represent and to help others who have brought their complaints to my attention because they do not have access to the Postmaster General except by mail. Delivery being uncertain, even his letter of explanation might not reach its destination for ten days or longer.
Without making any additional comments, I ask now for corrective action to be taken. The changeover to new equipment and a code system is no longer as satisfactory to the people who are paying for our postal system, the Canadian taxpayers.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-ALLEGED DELAY IN DELIVERY OF FIRST-CLASS MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the hon. member to give a few details about the complaints which he wanted to make. I thank him for doing so. I can assure him that if there is a special problem in Red Deer, we will immediately try to correct it.
I would like, however, to point out that it is somewhat unfair to judge the whole postal service by a few isolated cases. It may happen sometimes that Canadians find that their mail has been delayed. Out of 100 letters which they receive, one or two may be late. This does not mean that the postal service is bad. It means that twice out of a hundred times delivery has been delayed.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-ALLEGED DELAY IN DELIVERY OF FIRST-CLASS MAIL
speechtext:
I would like to add that of course the Post Office Department agrees that certain difficulties result sometimes in late delivery. In fact, there are four kinds of difficulties against which we come up all the time and which prevent the mail from reaching its destination as fast as we would like.
Firstly, transportation is of prime importance to us, and we largely depend on air service. For sure, our service is to a great extent adversely affected by bad weather conditions and delayed flights.
Secondly, the mail volume varies each day, and an abnormal increase in that volume will overtax our sorting and handling facilities.
Thirdly, we have identified 31 handling operations as sources of errors or delays, from the collection of mail to its delivery, and such inconveniences, I admit, happen.
Fourthly, our postal facilities are unfortunately obsolete in many Canadian cities, which makes the task of our employees quite difficult.
But the important thing, Mr. Speaker, is to say that we are trying very hard to correct and improve the situation.
Finally, I can assure the hon. member that our assured mail program is meeting with great success. I have here figures for the week ended May 25, and the results in his province of Alberta, for instance, are rather outstanding. Our investigation has shown that in Calgary our assured mail service had an efficiency rate of 98 per cent at the national level, namely for mail throughout the country, an efficiency rate of 99 per cent for regional mail, that is for mail in Alberta and of 89 per cent for local mail.
I agree with the hon. member that there may be a problem in the Red Deer and Calgary area. We will attempt to improve the situation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that on the whole, our assured mail service has an efficiency rate exceeding 95 per cent. Since more than 5 billion pieces of mail are handled per year, it can be said that, on the whole, the postal service is very efficient in Canada.
